Guru Angad Dev Veterinary and Animal Sciences University, Ludhiana, is committed in directing its core capabilities towards protecting the animals lives. As a special opportunity for our veterinarians to further commit to serve these speechless creatures, the university feels privileged to be always on beck and call to protect the animal population.

These views were expressed by Dr. V.K. Taneja, Vice-Chancellor, GADVASU, on the concluding day of the Wildlife Week. He added that our mandate was focussed on protecting public health, including research that explored inter-play among animals, people and the environment in a way to protect our eco-system. This is important not only for the people of Punjab and India, but also for all the areas of the world.

To survive pressure of more people and greater economic demands i.e these global challenges, we must also cross political and geographic boundaries to explore and share our understanding of how health and welfare of animals and humans relate to the general health of the planet.

On an average, about 20,000 cases are brought to the clinics for treatment or for surgical interventions. The College of Veterinary Science always measures up to these emergent needs by best serving the animals who are in distress. The college also caters to the needs by providing all requisite facilities for remedial measures to protect the endangered wild and zoo animals not only of Chhatbir Zoo but also by providing all diagnostic, medicinal and surgical coverage to animals in the zoo received from Himachal Pradesh.

The Dean College of Veterinary Science, Dr Simrat Sagar Singh informed that in order to provide better care to animal populace, the university has made concerted efforts in setting up and strengthening the centralized animal disease diagnostic laboratories, services at veterinary clinical services complex have been updated for providing round-the-clock facilities for diagnostic, medicinal and surgical intervention (s) for ameliorating the distress from animals.

Moreover, dramatic changes to histopathology/ immuno-pathology laboratories/clinical pathology laboratory/ and setting up of molecular biology laboratory etc. besides improvement of teaching facilities have given a new impetus to disease diagnosis to fulfill the key component of the college's integrated plan vis-a-vis for betterment of animal welfare.

However, a separate discipline on wildlife in the College of Veterinary Science for better protection of endangered wildlife needs to be initiated in veterinary sciences because of increasing poaching violations and the need to protect endangered species of animals. Focus should be on developing forensic medicine and forensic pathologists as they can help solve vetero-legal cases also. Efforts should be to develop this field as forensic psychology or criminology as it will help not only in detection of crimes but also in correctional methodology and rehabilitation of perpetrators and victims.

Heading: Sociology students of CBSE Class XII to have practical projects from 2010 - Indian Express
Content:
Chandigarh Administration signs MoUs with three companies

The Chandigarh Administration on Wednesday cleared the decks for setting up of an Education City at Sarangpur Institution Area, by signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with three parties.

Present on the occasion, UT Administrator S F Rodrigues said the project of Education City had been conceived to create world-class educational infrastructure, with the main focus on empowering children and sharpening their skills to make them professionally competent as well as confident individuals.

"Special emphasis has been laid on providing assistance, in the form of scholarships and low-cost quality education to committed and intelligent students belonging to the disadvantaged sections, who cannot afford to pay normal fees in other institutions," he said.

The three companies whose representatives signed MoUs with UT Home-cum-Education Secretary Ram Niwas included NMIMS (Narsee Monjee Institute of Management Studies), Chitkara Education Trust Chandigarh and Indian Express Newspapers (Mumbai) Limited.

Sources said the Education City also has effective linkages with the Rajiv Gandhi Information Technology Park, Film City, Theme Park and Medicity to share infrastructure support.

Rodrigues said being one of the mega projects to come up at the Sarangpur Institutional area on the UT's periphery, Education City will help in making Chandigarh a regional hub for extending support to the people of the region.

"Chandigarh is emerging as the regional hub to extend support to 60 million people of the region with its various new projects like the international airport, Mass Rapid Transport System, a super-fast train service between Delhi-Amritsar via Chandigarh and a modern terminal market for agriculture in the pipeline," added Rodrigues.

Dr N M Kondap, Vice Chancellor, NMIMS, assured to play an active role in various societal endeavours for building a prosperous life in the region.

Besides eminent educationists, Sanjay Kumar, Finance Secretary and Vivek Atray, Director Tourism and Public Relations were present on the occasion.

Heading: In Nayagaon, all constructions are unauthorised - Indian Express
Content:
Taking a note of the changing education trends, the Central Board of Secondary Education has decided to include a 20-mark practical project in sociology for students of Class XII.

It will be implemented in the Board examinations to be held in 2010. The project has been introduced in Class XI from this academic session onwards and shall be implemented for the students appearing in their Class XII examination next year.

New textbooks of sociology were introduced for Class XI in 2006-07 and for Class XII in 2007-08, in view of the revision of the syllabus according to the directions from the National Curriculum Framework 2005.

The CBSE through its circular has mentioned that sociology as a discipline is more a mode of inquiry rather than a fixed body of knowledge and hence the importance of the project.

Clarifying about the marks, the CBSE, has said that both the practical project as well as the theory paper shall be evaluated by external examiners.

Rakesh Sachdeva, Principal, DAV Senior Secondary School, Sector 15 said: "Sociology is a very interesting subject and projects like visiting old-age homes, slums, will provide an in depth knowledge of the subject. Students will be able to have a clearer picture of the social setup."

Vinita Arora, Principal, Bhavan Vidyalaya, Sector 27, said: "The practical aspect of any subject is a welcome move as it will give a better perspective to the students. Since the concept of education is moving more towards practical knowledge, students will definitely benefit from this."

Heading: ‘Unhealthy’ beep on cell phone radar - Indian Express
Content:
2 years on, Nayagaon Nagar Panchayat still 'powerless' to check encroachment

No construction existing in the Nayagaon municipal limits in the periphery of Chandigarh is authorised. Illegal constructions raised without getting building plans approved by competent authority have eaten up almost 80 per cent area of Karoran, 60 per cent of Kansal and 20 per cent of Nada villages, which constitute the Nayagaon Nagar Panchayat.

The facts came to light after Newsline filed an application under the Right to Information Act, 2005, seeking information from the civic body with regard to constructions in Nayagaon.

The civic body has not yet identified any encroachment in Nayagaon. Neither has it initiated any action against those responsible for raising the unauthorised structures. Reason: even two years after coming into being, the civic body does not have the power to regularise buildings, approving building plans and issuing no-objection certificates required for procuring power and water supply connections.

It may be mentioned that top politicians and bureaucrats own vast chunks of prime land and structures in the area.

In September, the Mohali Deputy Commissioner banned all new constructions in Nada and Karoran, besides refusing power, water supply connections and ration cards.

In his reply to the RTI application, the Public Information Officer of the Nayagaon Nagar Panchayat said with no major source of income, the civic body had to raise a loan of Rs 20 lakh from the 'cash-rich' Mandi Gobindgarh Municipal Council to meet its expenditure. The meagre development work taken place so far had been undertaken with the help of government grants.

In these two years, the Nayagaon Nagar Panchayat has received 27 building plans from Kansal area, but no plan could either be approved or rejected due to the restriction. The fee of Rs 29.73 lakh received with the building plans, however, was kept pending, which constituted a major income of the civic body since its establishment in October 2006.

Apart from that, the municipality earned Rs 52,000 from octroi on electricity, Rs 6,000 as rent and Rs 2.81 lakh from other sources to take its total revenue to Rs 53.12 lakh, the PIO said in his reply.

The total expenditure of Rs 46.01 lakh included Rs 22.25 lakh on salaries, Rs 3.53 lakh on stationery, office furniture and fixtures, Rs 16,000 on telephone and fax, Rs 1.28 lakh on miscellaneous, Rs 9.93 lakh on solid waste management, Rs 8.5 lakh on construction of streets and drains, besides Rs 1.05 lakh on streetlights.

The Nayagaon Nagar Panchayat received a grant of Rs 50,000 under the MP Land Area Development Fund in August 2007 for construction of a drain for waste disposal in Karoran. It could not be utilised due to restrictions imposed by the Punjab Land Preservation Act (PLPA).

Besides, the civic body got Rs 12.25 lakh grant for solid waste management and database computerisation in August and December 2007, of which Rs 3 lakh is yet to be spent. Another grant of Rs 6.19 lakh was received in June this year, of which Rs 1.37 lakh was spent on purchase of a water tanker, a carrier container system while Rs 4.75 lakh is lying unused.

Heading: Confident of winning from day one: Rana - Indian Express
Content:
A study with an aim to sensitise the general public on the ill effects of excessive cell-phone usage caused by electromagnetic radiation has been recently conducted at Panjab University (PU).

The study has shown that eggs exposed to four working mobiles become half-boiled in very little time. Not only this, the study has also informed that the Sectors 8, 9, 17, 18, 21, 23, 27, 30, 32, 33, 34, 35, 38, 44, 45, 46, 59 and 51 in the city are exposed to electromagnetic radiation released by the mobile phone towers, far more than the prescribed limit (as per a petition filed in the Supreme Court).

Prof V P Sharma, Dr R K Kohli and Dr H P Singh have conducted the study. While both Dr Kohli and Dr Singh are from the Department of Botany, Prof Sharma is from the Department of Zoology.

"We conducted research with an aim to sensitise the general public and make them aware of the fact that long hours of talking over cell phones can really damage the ears," Dr Kohli told Newsline.

The study has shown that mobile towers have two kinds of effects: thermal effect and non-thermal radiation effect. These effects are being studied simultaneously by the university on plants, honeybees and chicken eggs.

Meanwhile, the ENT department of the PGI has also conducted a similar study and found that spending long hours on the cell phone may result in loss of hearing. Some international studies also say that it can cause brain tumours.

Prof S Prabhakar, Head of the Department of Neurology, PGI, said, "The study has definitely shown that excessive cell phone usage is harmful. However, the exact nature of harm caused to the human body is yet to be ascertained."

Heading: Dimpy murder: bullet fired from Rocky’s pistol: police - Indian Express
Content:
For the fifth time in a row, Suresh Rana and his navigator Surendra K Nandal have won the Raid the Himalaya, the toughest motorsport event in the country. The Raid comprised about 2,050 kilometers of racing over 10 days through unbelievably harsh and difficult terrain, at a mean elevation of 4,000 meters and above, crossing eleven high passes in the Himalayas, and at places, mountains covered with snow as far as one could see.

The Raid has two categories - Extreme and Adventure. There were about 37 teams in the Extreme category, each comprising the driver and the navigator. And each team driving at breakneck speed through long stretches where the road was only a rocky track, and at times covered with thin ice too. Literally.

But Rana was a winner from Day One. On the second-last day of the Raid, when one of the tyres of his vehicle got punctured, Rana got delayed by five minutes. Not a cause to worry - Rana had a lead of 25 minutes over his nearest rival.

Talking to The Indian Express, Rana said he was confident of his win. "It was full on from the first day. The time when I faced a little bit of worry was when the gear lever of our vehicle broke, in the competitive stretch from Sarchu from Naki La. We had to drive on fourth gear all the way. But it's okay. We managed."

There is something common among winners. Complete confidence, for one. Ashish Moudgil, the 24-year-old from Kalka, was the overall winner among the mobikers - the guys for whom the Raid is the toughest. While those in four-wheelers have a certain degree of comfort, the bikers have to take everything head on - the bone-chilling winds of the Himalayas, the rain, the snow. Moudgil, 24, had also stood first in Raid 2005 and Raid 2007. Was he confident of his win this time too? "Definitely. Whoever comes to the start line comes there to win, not to stand second," says the bespectacled Moudgil, who works as a design engineer with Crompton Greaves in Bhopal.

In the Adventure category, which is a combination of speed, distance and time, the first prize went to Rajesh Chalana from Sri Ganganagar, and his navigator Rakesh Diwan. This was a hattrick for Chalana - he has topped the Adventure category in the Raid twice before.

As Vijay Parmar, president of the Himalayan Motorsport Association put it, "The rally is not just about racing cars on the most magnificent landscape in the world. It is a whole lot more to all those who are part of it. And your believing in a handful of ordinary people who are doing an extraordinary job." And most of these not-so-ordinary people will be back next year, for the unmatched high that the Raid offers them. Year after year.

Heading: Reports on arrest give civic leader ‘heart attack’ - Indian Express
Content:
The bullet, which killed gangster Prabjinder Singh alias Dimpy in Chandigarh two years ago, was fired from the same pistol that was recovered from Jaswinder Singh alias Rocky, an Uttar Pradesh-based gangster. Rocky was arrested in connection with the murder earlier this year. The Central Forensic Sciences Laboratory (CFSL) confirmed this, the Chandigarh Police said on Wednesday.

The US-made .45 bore pistol, which is issued to the soldiers of the US Army, was recovered from the possession of Rocky when he was arrested. He had allegedly given weapon to two shooters for eliminating Dimpy on July 7, 2006.

"During interrogation, Rocky confessed to giving his pistol to two shooters who were assigned the task of eliminating Dimpy. " said a senior police officer.

Heading: Two reasons to worry about city’s WiFi connections - Indian Express
Content:
Cops confirm one more picked up for IM links but cannot name the catch

Another person from Pune has been picked up for alleged links with SIMI and Indian Mujahideen. The police wouldn't identify him, some local newspapers made a guess, and the man they identified - a corporator - was so shocked that he suffered a heart attack, his family said.

Police Commissioner Satyapal Singh on Thursday confirmed that one person has been picked up. "We don't have the name of this person. We even don't know which agency picked him up," Singh said.

Even before his confirmation, local newspapers on Thursday saying the person was corporator Javed Shiekh from Pimpri-Chinchwad Municipal Corporation, picked up by the Mumbai police for questioning on his alleged links with IM.

Journalists rushed to Sheikh's house, where his family said he was admitted to Diwan Hospital at Nigdi. "The news of his supposed arrest is false. Javed suffered a heart attack after seeing TV reports linking him to Indian Mujahideen. Javed has a lot of enemies who are spreading lies about him," said Javed's sister Meenaj Shaikh and mother Hazra Shaikh

Sheikh's aides initially did not allow journalists to speak to him at the hospital. They said the reports were the handiwork of Sheikh's political rivals, with elections round the corner.

Later, the corporator himself spoke to the media.

"False information has been spread about me about my connections with radical outfits and that I have been arrested. If such a thing can happen to a corporator, what can common citizens expect?" he said.

"My sister and mother went to the Nigdi police station to complain against the false news appearing in the news paper and channels. But the police paid no heed to them. They told her to file a case against the newspapers," Shiekh said further.

He described his credentials: "In spite of being a Muslim, I was the one who brought to the notice of the police the counterfeit currency scam in Nigdi in which Bangladeshis were involved. These Bangladeshis might have connections with the ISI and other radical outfits. This was exposed only because of me, not because of any police intelligence."

Meanwhile, the Mumbai police have formed a special team to investigate the transfer of funds to the arrested suspects' accounts. Mumbai police are on a look out for those who were funding the SIMI and Indian Mujahideen modules in Pune.

Heading: Second, no launch on Games route, but ‘safe’ link at venue - Indian Express
Content:
First, hacking is easy, detection difficult

The recent hacking of Wi-Fi connections by terrorists has underscored the difficulty in securing such networks. "Unlike bomb blasts carried out by terrorists, hacking is a hidden and difficult-to-trace activity. Tampering into others' computer systems does not leave any tangible trace," said Sudam Choure, chief coordinator of Pune police's cyber committee.

"There is nothing like 'ethical hacking'. People with a criminal intent can easily get trained in 'ethical hacking' and use their knowledge for criminal activities," Choure said.

Mansoor Asghar Peerbhoy, the IT executive arrested from the city, has been described as the head of an Indian Mujahideen module that hacked Wi-Fi networks to send terror mails before and after serial blasts. He had taken up a course in ethical hacking.

Deputy Commissioner of police (cyber crime) Rajendra Dahale agreed. "Use of Wi-Fi technology for crime is increasing, as it is difficult to trace the hackers."

The police have started encouraging IT firms to secure their Wi-Fi networks. Police Commissioner Satyapal Singh said, "We have urged them to be alert and take measures to secure their Wi-Fi networks."

Choure suggested that audits of systems security be carried out at regular intervals. "The intelligence of hackers can never be underestimated. Security systems should go through a number of layers to check the authenticity of the user. That could curb hacking to some extent," he said.

One can hack into a system from a cyber café and the Pune Central Cyber Café Association has tried to put a safeguard in place. Association president Rahul Pokale said, "We don't let any user inside a café without first asking for an identity proof such as a driving licence or PAN card, with the person's photograph on it. We keep a photocopy. If anyone refuses to produce such proof, we not only deny them access but sometimes even inform the police if the customer is adamant."

At the Balewadi sports complex, the police said the Fi connections are well-protected. "We willl not allow visitors, expect authorised journalists and VIPs, to carry laptops into the sports complex," the Commissioner of Police said.

Heading: Pratibha in town to launch soft loans for women - Indian Express
Content:
A Wi-Fi network is being put in place at the Commonwealth Youth Games (CYG) venue in Balewadi but the network planned for the CYG route from the airport to the venue is not yet complete. The Pimpri-Chinchwad Municipal Corporation (PCMC), which is providing the network at the venue, describes it as "secure".

"Only authorised users will have access to the connections," said Neelkanth Poman, IT head of PCMC. These would mean players and officials involved with the Games.

"We are following police guidelines. Users will be given a login, a password and an identity proof. The Wi-Fi network will be functional within a 4 km radius of the venue but only authorised users will be access it We are also having the security checked by a third party," he added.

"With the help of Infrastructure Leasing and Financial Services Limited (IL&FS), we have been able to complete the task of providing the Wi-Fi cover. However, it is still being tested," PCMC commissioner Asheesh Sharma said.

The Wi-Fi network on the CYG route had been undertaken by the Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC). "The road development work fell behind schedule, which is why we could not complete the unwiring of the CYG route," said Anupam Saraph, chief information officer (CIO) of the PMC. "When we started discussing this plan months ago, six firms showed an interest. However, when they saw that the work was not over, they expressed reservations," he added.

Sujit Singh, official of Microsense Pvt Ltd, the company through which PMC launched the 'Unwired Pune' project, said, "The terrain has to be good, which is not so on the CYG route due to the incomplete road construction till recently. That created a major obstacle. Besides, the feasibility of the project needs to be checked, as the sportspersons will anyway be provided with Wi-Fi facility at the complex."

Heading: Civic body ready to supply the tenant info that the police need - Indian Express
Content:
President Pratibha Patil will be in Pune on Friday to launch a scheme of loans at 4 per cent interest for women's self-help groups (SHGs). At a function in the city, she will hand over loans to two SHGs from Pune and one each from Solapur, Satara and Nashik.

Nearly 17 lakh women from rural areas and 1,42,218 SHGs will benefit from the scheme. "The 4 per cent interest replaces the existing 9-11 per cent. Around 45,000 SHGs will get Rs 50,000, 72,000 will get Rs 1 lakh and 18,000 SHGs Rs 2 lakh disbursement. These groups will be eligible for higher loans once they repay these loans on time," said an official of the women and child welfare department.

The loans are from Bank of India, Bank of Maharashtra, Solapur Gramin Bank and State Bank of India. The banks will not lose as the state will pay the remaining amount they would have earned as interest.

"The aim being to help these women have easier access to credit and help improve their livelihood. The interest subsidy will cost the government nearly Rs 129.01 crore over three years," the official said.

Bank officials are confident of repayment, going by the past record of the women. "The loan repayment of these SHGs is 90 per cent and we have no issues in giving them the amount," said a senior officer from Bank of Maharashtra. An officer from a district coo-perative bank in Pune said the loans would inspire the women to do well in business, which would ensure better returns and regular repayment.

Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh have been giving interest subsidies to such organisations.

The beneficiaries are delighted with the development. Manisha Kale from Pune's Garib Nawaz Bachat Gat, which will be getting nearly Rs 2 lakh, said they would start work on dairy soon, aiming at high returns and quick repayment.

Heading: Yesterday once more - Indian Express
Content:
If property owners and real estate agents fail to furnish details of their tenants, the civic administration is ready to supply the police with al the information at its disposal. Only, the police have not yet asked, though they have launched a drive against owners who don't supply tenant details.

The Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) keeps a record of 5 lakh properties, of which 10,000 are listed as having been rented out or used for some other purpose other than as the owners' residences. If the owner himself lives on the property, the civic body gives a 40 per cent rebate on property tax; whenever an owner claims this, it is verified by civic inspectors. In case of new properties, the civic administration verifies all information with the developer.

"Around 2 per cent of the 5 lakh properties in the city don't avail the facility of tax rebate. These are considered to be either rented or being used for some non-residential purpose by the owner," said Vilas Kanade, PMC tax assessment and collection officer

"The information with the PMC can be useful to the police. We are ready to share the information, but there is no formal request from the police so far," PMC additional commissioner M S Devnikar said.

Additional Commissioner of Police Rajinder Singh is open to the idea. "We were unaware that such information is available with the PMC. The police are ready to approach them."

The PMC will soon seek details of tenant information being collected by the police so that it could be matched with the data with the PMC. "It is not possible for the PMC to recheck the status of the property, but a comparison of the information can always be made," Kanade said.

The ACP said the police would not mind sharing the information.

The ongoing drive against property owners for failing to submit tenant information has taken a back seat for now, with the police too busy with security for the Commonwealth Youth Games.

Heading: Stringing sargam - Indian Express
Content:
Actor Madhav Vaze, popularly known as Shyam from the national award-winning film Shyamachi Aai makes a comeback with Shobha Yatra

At a time when education was considered the sole scale of judging a child's calibre, television was yet to be invented and terminologies like TRP, readership, and viewership were still to capture the non-existing market, Madhav Vaze, blazed the silver screen as a child star way back in 1953. Crowning the achievement Shyamachi Aai was the fact that the film went on to bag the first national award and catapulted all its actors into instant fame.

Yet Vaze decided to take a long break of over 20 years from acting and concentrate on directing plays. And now he returns to take centresatge through the play — Shobha Yatra. "I am playing the character of Mahatma Gandhi in the play. I had no plans of getting into acting but when director Ravi Sambare approached me for the role in the play, the character of Mahatma Gandhi tempted me to take up the offer," smiles Vaze.

The character of Shyam in Shyamachi Aai gave Vaze his identity. Even today, he is remembered as the Shyam of that film. "After that film people always thought that I would take up acting as a profession. I too was interested in acting right up to my college days. But that's when I discovered the thrill of direction and realised that filmmaking is a director's medium. Infact my directorial ventures date back to my college days when I directed plays for my college at Purushottam Karandak and won the best director award for two consecutive years," adds he.

After Purushottam, direction became the sole focus for Vaze who directed a number of well-known plays like Preshit by Madgulkar, Hriday by Shyam Manohar, Tughlak by Girish Karnad and a few based on the stories of Vijaya Rajadhyaksha. Vaze who has of late developed an interest in interpretation of plays observes, "I personally feel that the importance of diction and the language used for drama is deteriorating. Acharya Atre read and studied the book for two years before making the film Shyamachi Aai. But today's fast paced life does not give the director the time to think. And this reduced thinking span has affected the thought process of filmmakers and theatre personalities. But I must say that even today, there are quality writers and filmmakers who even in a short span give justice to the script."

A star since an early age, Vaze expresses concern over the growing attention towards child artistes due to television shows and advertisements. "My school teachers and parents made me realise that I was talented. But what they also taught me was that if I was a talented actor, children around me were extraordinary in other activities like academics, sports and so on. This kept me grounded because I never felt like a star and thought like all other skills, acting is just another skill. Today's children are getting a lot of attention. But the ones to be blamed are parents and no one else. With a glimpse of slightest of talent, the parents expect their children to reach the skies. I personally feel that if the child is talented, you need to give time to nurture the talent and at the right time the child will peak. I just have one suggestion for today's parents, which is what my father told me — let your head touch the skies, but your feet should always remain on the ground," he concludes.

Heading: Small talk - Indian Express
Content:
Overwhelmed by the hospitality and the traditional welcome, countries at CYG are all charged to display their skills

If first impression is the last impression then we've made a good long lasting one. Be it the smallest of the teams to the biggest ones, Indian hospitality has won hearts of every commonwealth countries. In a diverse nation with diversities of their own, the representatives of the countries share their first impressions along with the specialties that their teams are equipped with.

Vanuatu is one of the countries with as less as six athletes participating in the Commonwealth Youth Games and that too for the first time. According to Anolyn Lulu, table tennis coach, Vanuatu, "We will be participating in table tennis and athletics. We are overwhelmed by the hospitality of Indians. We were aware of the fact that Indians are warm and loving people but with the grand welcome that we received, we even after being the smallest of the teams felt that we are important and our presence is special."

Team Malaysia consists of over 40 athletes and 16 officials. With a number of Indians in the Malaysian team, Indian culture is not new to Malaysia. This however makes their approach even different as Chua Hong Tam, athletic official, Malaysia, says, "We landed in India on October 8 and were welcomed in a grand and a special way at Mumbai. We had heard about the Indian culture in Malaysia but what was exciting was to be a part of traditional events like wearing the turban, participating in Bhangra and so on. "An important and an interesting feature of the Malaysian team are the T-shirts that boast the theme - save tiger, by printing tiger-like stripes on their T-shirts. Preman Parameswaran, head quarter staff member, Team Malaysia says, "This theme is designed specifically by a bunch of Malaysian students to go with Jigrr."

While most of them have been talking about the hospitality, team UK is overwhelmed by the pace at which Indians work. One of the biggest teams at the Commonwealth Youth Games, with as many as 106 sportspersons, team England considers boxing as their USP. "When we came here a couple of days ago, there were a number of roads still under construction but today I am surprised to see that most of the construction work is over and roads ready," says Gannon Michael, athletic official, Team England.

The energetic atmosphere at CYG venue is what that has impressed Team Australia, which has come with as many as 128 members. According to Ashleigh Stevenson, team member, "We are happy to be a part of this event. Considering the competition between the cricket teams of both the countries, performing well becomes our responsibility. The venue and the atmosphere here is very energetic and we hope that we make a lasting impression."

A small yet capable team of eight athletes is Kiribati Islands. "We are a small nation. We will be participating in all the games here. We had heard about the diversity of this country but yesterday was the first time we experienced it. I must say that Indians are very helpful people," says Tewati Tetau, athletic official, team Kiribati.

After playing a kind and good host, India is now all set to play tough opponent for the participants.

Heading: Security beefed up for CYG; Cops issue guidelines - Indian Express
Content:
Draping beauties
Saree, the nine-yard couture, is a beautiful attire that not only reflects tradition but also enhances style, grace, beauty and elegance of a woman. Fuel the fashion store at Connaught Place at Bundgarden Road, recently held an interesting saree promo event, for the upcomping festive and wedding season. Well-known designers like Masala works, nidha for skin and Ravage from Mumbai and Delhi displayed their saree collection. Tunics, salwar suits, shoes, bags and earings were also at display for the event. There was nail art and express manicure done by La Clinique, Koregaon Park, while Bharti goel gave complimentary sessions on innovative ways to drape a saree for the visitors. Fuel will be having a large variety of tunics and other Indian wear in the store for the Diwali season.

Shot and sweet
Open Space, the outreach initiative of the Centre for Communication and Development studies (CCDS), Pune, has organised a two day film festival titled Insights and Aspirations in collaboration with the Department of Sociology, University of Pune at Namdeo Sabhagriha Auditorium, Pune University. Starting today, the festival will screen a wide variety of selected documentaries like Manpasand - The Perfect Match by director Dhwani Desai, The Cheese & the Worms by Haruyo Kato, Leap Frog by Nandita Das, Taaza Khabar by Bishakha Dutta and so on. The films have been made recently and have not been screened in Pune earlier. Entry is free on a first-come-first-served basis.

Heading: PCB to tighten security for ‘Grand Carnival’ - Indian Express
Content:
No mobile phones, laptops and cameras. All those who enter the CYG zone have to leave all those gadgets behind and even eatables. The Pune Police in a bid to provide maximum security and ensure smooth going of CYG games came out on Thursday with strict guidelines.

Speaking at a press conference here the Commissioner of Police, Satyapal Singh said, "People will not be allowed to bring cameras and mobile phones into the games venue. Even though the entire complex has a Wi-Fi connection for security reasons only game officials, police personnel and the media personnel will be allowed to carry laptops to the venue."

People who are sick or are suffering from any ailment will have to get themselves checked by team of doctors who will be present at the venue. "Only after their certification that the person is genuinely unwell and suffers from a particular type of ailment will he be allowed to take his medicines inside the complex."

Over 3000 police personnel will be deployed all over the city and four teams of the CRPF and two teams of the SRPF will man the venue. "We are also coordinating with the army to ensure that there be enough personnel around the city. The entire games venue, athletes village and parking zones will be manned by CCTV cameras capable of storing data up to 20 days. Contingency plans and emergency evacuation plans have also been put into place and the rehearsals for the same, have also been done."

Singh said, "Total of 10 Bomb Detection and Disposal Squad (BDDS) will be pressed into service apart from two reserve BDDS. As far as 22 striking teams will be ready, comprising of CRPF, SRPF, and the Pune Police. Further there will be 30 Nakabandi points and 40 chowks in the city, which will be guarded by the police. About 300 extra officers and 1200 police personnel have been called in for assisting the present team. Also other than the VVIP's everyone (including the VIP's) will be frisked and made to pass through DFMD's (door frame metal detectors) and searched Using HFMD's (hand held metal detectors). Expressing concern over the ongoing construction work at the CYG venue he said, "We have been assured by the officials at the venue that all work will be completed by October 10. We are hopeful that the work is done by then as it will give us a clear picture, and will be important from the security point of view too."

Heading: Meanwhile, mixed reactions to ‘No construction plan’ - Indian Express
Content:
In the wake of the recent arrests of terror suspects from parts of the city, the Pune Cantonment Board (PCB) is planning to beef up security measures in and around M G Road for the three-day 'Grand Carnival', a special Walking Plaza to be held from October 14-16, PCB vice president Prasad Kedari said on Thursday.

Addressing media persons, Kedari said the PCB in collaboration with 'BRAND Knew', an event management firm, is organising the event during the Commonwealth Youth Games (CYG), which is being held at Balewadi Sports Complex here from October 12-18. The event will go ahead as planned, he added.

"The board administration will leave no stone unturned to ensure a watertight security system during the Grand Carnival. Ample security arrangements are already in place. Further, in view of the recent arrests, additional safety precautions will be taken," Kedari said.Apart from the city police, Corps of Military Police (CMP) personnel would also be deployed to maintain law and order. Metal detectors would be set up on all strategic entry and exit points to M G Road, Kedari said, adding that the PCB had roped in around 25 persons as traffic wardens to facilitate smooth flow of traffic during the event and throughout the CYG itinerary. "We are well-prepared and expect the event to pass without any unpleasant incident. Hopefully, the 'Grand Carnival' will be a big hit with citizens," he said.Reiterating this viewpoint, BRAND Knew director Amreysh Dubey said, "The Grand Carnival aims at sending out a positive message and commemorate the CYG, of which the city is the proud host. Enthusiastic participation of citizens will ensure that the Carnival is a grand success." Expressing confidence in the security arrangements made by the PCB, Dubey said, "We are confident about the security arrangements . Further, the company will hire private security guards who will be deployed in and around the venue." BRAND Knew is investing around Rs 65 lakh into the Carnival, out of which the PCB will contribute Rs 35 lakh. The remaining amount will be raised through sponsors. Elaborating on the Grand Carnival, Dubey said, "The three-day celebration will get going on October 14. Music, dance, laser shows and bicycle stunts have been planned." When contacted, PCB chief executive officer S K Sardana said, "The M G Road region will sport a festive look for the Grand Carnival and during the CYG. Foolproof security measures have been planned."

Heading: Pediatric Kidney Diseases Registry throws light on kidney failure in children - Indian Express
Content:
The directive issued by the commissioner of police asking builders, who have construction sites near the CYG venue, to stop construction work from October 11 to October 18 drew mixed reactions. When some builders appreciated the idea, some opposed it.

Commissioner of Police, Satyapal Singh addressing a press conference on Thursday had said, "We are asking all the builders who have construction projects near the CYG venue, to ensure that they do not ferry the construction materials during the day time between 8 am to 8 pm. We also hope that they will not carry out any construction work during the above mentioned days near the games venue." Reacting to the direction issued by the police commissioner Nitin Nyati, of the Nyati Group said, "Speaking as a builder the decision to halt construction work at sites along the venue, is not a good idea. However, in the spirit of the games and the fact that by hosting the game Pune will be on the international map are factors for supporting the police directive. Even though the ferrying of materials is being disallowed in the morning it is going to be open in the evening and at night so at least the builders will be able to work then."

Vasudevan R of Vascon Builders, who has an ongoing project at Baner Road said, "The idea to stop construction work near the venue is not the best of ideas. Builders will stand to lose during the time period. I am of the opinion that work on projects that are located close to the venue should not stop." But Hemant Naiknavre of Naiknavre and associates chose to call the police decision as 'sensible '. "Since all ferrying work will be done after 8 pm in the evening the idea that the roads will not be clogged unnecessarily during the morning, due to the heavy vehicles ferrying the construction materials, seems sensible. Stopping construction work during the event is not a big issue. It might even give the workers working at these sites a welcome break." Nitin Nyati also said, "The smallest of projects along these roads could lose up to a couple of lakhs during if the work is stopped. Bigger projects might lose more but still I personally feel it is a good experience for the city."

Heading: BVU introduces Doctor of Pharmacy course - Indian Express
Content:
A long-felt need to understand what causes kidney failure in children has led to the setting up of a National Pediatric Kidney Diseases Registry, which in its interim report has shown that 45 per cent of at least 300 children with chronic kidney failure had developed an obstruction or a urinary tract infection. The disease could have been prevented had it been diagnosed early in childhood.

With this objective, a National Pediatric Kidney Diseases Registry was started in collaboration with Indian Society of Nephrology. The registry, which operates at Nadiad, Gujarat, has data being collected from six centres including the Armed Forces Medical College (AFMC) here, All India Institute of Medical Science, New Delhi and hospitals in Mumbai, Chennai and Bangalore.

According to Col Madhuri Kanitkar, head of the Department of Paediatrics, AFMC, who has organised a conference on the issue from October 10-12, the data from the registry was an eye-opener as it shows that 44 per cent children are developing renal failure due to obstructive or reflux nephropathy, both of which can be diagnosed early in childhood and the kidneys protected to some extent. With the ever-increasing burden of chronic kidney disease and lack of resources to ensure dialysis and transplant for all, there is a need to focus on preventive strategies, said Kanitkar. The AFMC and Command Hospital has a paediatric nephrology unit since 2001 for children of service personnel and civilians and has over 700 children on follow-up.

Kidney diseases, both acute and chronic in children are a significant cause of disability and death, requiring a specialised approach to diagnosis and management.

The child with a kidney ailment has been hitherto a neglected entity owing to lack of adequate expertise amongst general pediatricians regarding renal disorders and problems faced by adult nephrologists in handling small children with kidney problems, he said.

The Indian Pediatric Nephrology Group, which has been re-christened the Indian Society of Pediatric Nephrology (ISPN), will host its conference from October 10-12 at AFMC, Pune. Around 200 national and international faculty and delegates are attending the conference. Experts in pediatric nephrology from abroad who are participating in the conference include Dr Dr Franz Schaefer (Germany), Dr Yap Hui Kim (Singapore), Dr Patrick Walker (USA) , Dr MJ Dillon (UK) and Dr Alok Kalia (USA). Dr R N Srivastava (New Delhi), Dr B R Nammalwar (Chennai), Dr Kumud Mehta (Mumbai) and Dr Arvind Bagga ( New Delhi).

Maj Gen G Rajagopal, Dean and Dy Commandant AFMC will be the chief guest for the Inaugural function to be held on October 11 at the Bharadwaja auditorium at AFMC. The conference will focus on preventable causes of chronic kidney disease in children.

Heading: Equipping the poor with entrepreneurial skills: BYST leads the way - Indian Express
Content:
The Bharati Vidyapeeth University (BVU) has introduced a six-year Doctor of Pharmacy course (PharmD) based on the US Doctor of Pharmacy course, which will be recognised internationally. The students completing the course will be able to prescribe medicines to patients.

"We got the permission just a month back when the course was formally approved by the Union Government," said Shivajirao Kadam, vice chancellor of BVU who is also a member of Pharmaceutical Council of India. "The course will open new avenues for the students, who want to pursue career in pharmacy," he said.

At present, the four-year bachelor of pharmacy (BPharm) is the only option available for the students. PharmD is an integrated six-year course that gives students an authority to prescribe medicines to patients. "The admission procedure has already started and we expect an intake of 30 students for the first year," said Kadam.

Kadam said as the degree is recognised internationally, students could have option either to work in India or abroad. "The present degree course in pharmacy doesn't allow the candidate to prescribe medicines to patients. The PharmD course is inclusive of a two-year internship in hospital, by which students will learn how to prescribe medicines," said Kadam.

"The course enable the students to even prescribe medicines to doctors. In countries like the US and UK, pharmacist and doctors collectively prescribe medicines by consulting each other. It avoids the mishaps like over dose," said Kadam.

The BVU is the third university in the country to introduce the course. Kadam said that the students who had passed BPharm course are eligible for admission in PharmD. "A three-year postgraduate baccalaureate course will also be available for BPharm students," he added.

Heading: CYG baton received at Bank of Maharashtra - Indian Express
Content:
To organise seminar on October 15

The journey from being a caddy in an automobile workshop, earning a menial amount of Rs 300 per month, to an entrepreneur with an annual turnover of Rs 25-30 lakh, took Mustaffa Yasim Sayyed just five years. At 27, Mustaffa is now the proud owner of a firm that deals in sales and servicing of electrical water pumps – thanks to an initiative by the Bharatiya Yuva Sakthi Trust (BYST), a non-profit organisation founded by the legendary JRD Tata in 1991.

BYST's programme includes supporting young entrepreneurs from the underprivileged sections of society by supplementing finance up to Rs five lakh along with training, support, monitoring and networking. It also supports marketing, training, seed capital, counselling, mentoring and networking.

"Our vision is to motivate the youth and create employment for others, thereby transforming job seekers into job creators. Our success rate is 95 per cent," said Sudha Santhanam, chairperson, Entrepreneur Selection Panel (ESP) committee, M G Road, BYST. The organisation along with Mudhol Land Holdings (MLH) will hold a seminar on 'Spirit of Entrepreneurship programme for Dynamic Youth' on October 15 at Ghorpadepeth Udyan.

Vijaysinh Maurya, managing director of MLH and vice chairman of ESP said BYST focuses on youth in the age group of 18-35, who have viable business ideas. "The organisation has a tie-up with Bank of Baroda. During the past 15 years, it has expanded to six regions including Delhi, rural Haryana, Chennai, Pune, Hyderabad and rural Maharashtra. It has financed 1,500 entrepreneurs, creating employment for 15,000 people," Maurya said.

Surendra Agarwal, chairman of the M G Road chapter of BYST, said the organisation aims at creating jobs and fostering prosperity. "The organisation has made almost 1,000 entrepreneurs out of which almost 50 are millionaires. It has created wealth of around Rs 50,380 million," he said.

Heading: New diversion points for heavy vehicles - Indian Express
Content: The chairman and managing director of Bank of Maharashtra (BoM), Allen Pereira received the youth baton relay of Commonwealth Games at bank's head office at Shivajinagar when it arrived in the city. The bank is the sole official banker for the third Commonwealth Youth games 2008. Chairman CYG, Suresh Kalmadi, hockey player Dhanraj Pillai, other officials of CYG and BoM were also present on the occasion. The BoM float accompanied the relay team on the entire route.

Heading: Girija Godbole bags Gates Trust Scholarship - Indian Express
Content:
Heavy vehicles coming from Mumbai towards Pune and going to areas like Satara, Nagar and Solpaur during the Commonwealth Youth Games (CYG), which is being held in the city from October 12-18 will have to take diversions.The first diversion point will be at Urse Toll Naka (Pune-Mumbai Expressway) and the second at Talegaon Phata (ahead of Urse Toll Naka). Heavy vehicles, particularly those carrying hazardous chemicals, going towards Solapur will have to go from the Urse Toll Naka towards Talegaon Phata and go towards Talegaon Dabhade Chowk and then take the Shikhrapur-Nhavra Phata-Chowphula Marg.

Heavy vehicles going towards Nagar will have to go from the Urse Toll Naka towards Talegaon Phata, proceed towards Talegaon Dabhade Chowk and Chakan and then take the Shikhrapur Marg. Heavy vehicles going towards Satara will have to go from the Urse Toll Naka towards Talegaon Phata, proceed to Talegaon Dabhade Chowk and then head for Chakan- Shikhrapur-Nhavra Phata-Chowphula-Moregaon-Nira-Lonad Shirval Marg.

Heading: City bids adieu to goddess amid fear and chaos - Indian Express
Content:
Mirror image
Imran Khan is not only following in uncle Aamir's footsteps but he also seems to have donned the same pair of shoes — the similarities just don't seem to end. The lad has been on his toes ever since the release of Kidnap. He has been travelling across the length and breadth of the country in attempt to salvage his film Kidnap. Says Dhilin Mehta, producer from Shree Ashtavinayak Cine Vision, "Imran, like Aamir, believes in doing everything with sincerity and gives his 100 per cent to whatever he does. He was very cooperative and would turn up for all promotional events on time despite his overnight rise to stardom." It won't be long before Imran's mirror has Aamir mamu staring back at him.

Diamonds and baubles
KIM Sharma says that New York is her favourite shopping destination as it houses all international brands. The actress, who's of late only visible at social dos, says that she makes frequent trips to the Big Apple and usually shops at Bloomingdales and Canal Street for clothes and Clay Pot for her sparkling diamonds. But all we wish to know, darling, is: where is all the money coming from?

South speak
ARJAN Bajwa is working hard to impress the South Indian audiences. The model-turned-actor has signed three South Indian films and is now learning martial arts. "The directors down South do not like to use body doubles — the actors are expected to do their own stunts," he explains. Bajwa will star alongside Nagarjuna, NT Ramarao's son Balakrishnan and South superstar Mohan Babu in his forthcoming projects. The actor is also learning the local languages, which seems to be the most difficult task. "Ask me to jump from a 50-storey building; I would find it easier than learning Telegu," he laughs.

Heading: Future City? With zero progress  on ground, it’s still a pipedream - Indian Express
Content:
"This was the most unorganised Sangat Darshan programme in the whole state. It seems the local leaders did not do their homework well," said Chief Minister Parkash Singh Badal at Mann Resorts in Haibowal on Friday.

Earlier, the CM had categorically stated that he will take up only development-related issues during the programme. But to his surprise and irritation, a majority of the grievances were related to personal problems such as unemployment, pensions and property.

Badal pulled up his party workers for not scrutinising the type of problems to be redressed on the occasion. Also, many villagers had come to air their grievances even though it was specifically stated that the Sangat Darshan was for urban residents only. Villages will be taken up in a second round after a few days, said party workers. Sources said the local councillors had to hold a meeting in their area to apprise residents about the concept of the Sangat Darshan but most failed to do so. Badal also said that a special camp to take up pension-related problems will be held on October 16.

Heading: Schools turn ‘smart’: Upload results on net - Indian Express
Content:
Work on 13 projects, chalked out in the last one-and-a-half-year, yet to begin

'Future City' was the epithet given to Mohali by Shiromani Akali Dal president Sukhbir Badal but it seems mere rhetoric now.

In the last one-and-a-half-year, the Punjab Infrastructure Development Board (PIDB) has chalked out 13 projects, estimated to cost Rs 4,843 crore. But work is yet to take off on any of the projects.

Official documents of PIDB, in possession of Chandigarh Newsline, reveal that construction of a state-of-the-art multi-storied bus terminal-cum-commercial complex and Institute of Hotel Management (IHM) in Mohali was abandoned after the successful bidders failed to fulfill the terms and conditions of the agreements. The total estimated cost of both projects was Rs 300 crore.

Bus terminal-cum-commercial complex
The construction, operation and maintenance of an air-conditioned bus terminal-cum-commercial complex in Phase VI for 90 years was awarded to M/s Akruti City Limited, Mumbai, at the highest bid of Rs 201 crore (against a reserve price of Rs 150 crore) on August 21. The company, however, failed to submit performance security of Rs 10 crore and 50 per cent of the upfront consideration of the total bid amount. Also, the project development fee of Rs 1.25 crore was not paid and the concession agreement within the stipulated period was not signed.
The project is proposed to come up on design, build, operate and transfer (DBOT) basis.

Institute of Hotel Management
For the Rs 150-crore IHM project, the successful bidder M/s Neesa Leisure Limited failed to fulfill the terms and conditions mentioned in the letter of award issued on June 25. Accordingly, a proposal security of Rs 10 lakh, submitted by way of unconditional and irrevocable bank guarantee, has been encashed by the PIDB. The abandoned project involved the construction, operation and maintenance of the institute with a three-star hotel facility for 45 years on a DBOT basis.

Other projects
Another two much-touted projects — IT Tower and Punjab Habitat Centre — have not found any takers yet.
The Rs 150-crore Tower for Information Technology and IT Enabled Services was proposed to come up on a build, operate and transfer basis for a concession period of 90 years. But PIDB's wait for a bidder seems unending as the last date of receipt of bids (August 7) passed uneventfully. Same is the case with the Rs 175-crore Punjab Habitat Centre. No bid was received for this project even after the last date (September 15).
A PIDB official said the Executive Committee will decide on the future course of action regarding the abandoned projects in its next meeting.

Heading: PU professor selected as INSA fellow - Indian Express
Content:
Notes in the school diary, the traditional method to update parents about various upcoming activities, seem to have been overtaken by the latest technological devices. From uploading results on the internet to sending SMSes to parents about their ward's performance, schools have adopted 'smart' communication all the way.

"Every one has a cellphone these days and sending a message is convenient and quick. Now, we inform parents about all school events either through e-mail or SMS. Even the results of house tests are sent via SMS," said Madhu Bahl, principal of KBDAV School, Sector 7.

Some schools have even started posting the annual examination results on their website. "From last year, we have started uploading the annual results on the internet so that students can conveniently check their scores at home," said a teacher of Government Model Senior Secondary School, Sector 16. "This way, the students cannot escape without showing their marks to their parents," she smiles.

Besides this one-way channel of communication, some principals prefer using the cellphone to stay in touch with students. Rakesh Sachdeva, principal of DAV Model School, Sector 15, said: "I have given my mobile number to students so that they can contact me whenever the need arises. The other day, some students were held up in a traffic jam near Kalka and messaged that they would be unable to report in time for an examination. So I allowed them extra time to take the test when they arrived. I believe, SMS and e-mail are very efficient means to reach out to parents as well as students."

Heading: ‘Namesake engages the reader in a poignant tale of those living in an alien country’ - Indian Express
Content:
Dr K N Pathak, Professor Emeritus and former Vice-Chancellor of Panjab University, has been elected as a fellow by the Indian National Science Academy (INSA) on Thursday. Dr Pathak is the only professor who has been honored by INSA in the subject of physics from the states of Punjab, Haryana, Himachal and Jammu & Kashmir. Heading: Earth Matters - Indian Express
Content:
Upon getting my hands on Jhumpa Lahiri's The Namesake, I though it would be another tale of the Indian diaspora. No doubt the book is about an emigrant Bengali couple and their life in an alien country, but Lahiri's expressions have turned it into a marvellous read.

The tale of the Ganguli's: Ashok and Ashima, is no different from the other NRIs, who carve their lives in an unknown land but remain rooted to their traditions. The couple wants their children to grow up in the land of opportunities, but at the same time, try their best to retain their Indian identity.

The Namesake is the story of Gogol, who is named after a Russian writer, who is a favourite of his father. Gogol struggles with his unusual name and in his attempt to find an identity, he becomes a rebel.

From changing his name to dating a foreigner, he does it all. He is, however, aware that his activities hurt his parents, but since he is a confused desi, he must do it all befotre finally finding his moorings.

In a moving scene, Gogol's father Ashok, gifts him a book by a Russian author, his namesake, hoping he will be able to understand the significance of the book in his life.

But Gogol, like the typical teenager, is preoccupied with rock music and is indifferent to his father's feelings. The books engages the reader in the poignant tale of those living in exile, the silence of which, is broken by a late night telephone call from India, announcing someone's death or illness.

It ends on a balanced note, wherein, while Ashima, now a widow, decides to spend her time shuttling between America and Calcutta and Gogol, now thirty-two and divorced, discovers in his father's gift of short stories, a temporary reconciliation with his name and the heritage he had rejected.

Heading: Stage for change - Indian Express
Content:
Focusing on eco-centric subjects, filmmakers turn environment activists in frames of green

We are all slaves of convenience, shutting our eyes at gory sights, blocking our ears on piercing screams, silencing our voice for fear of a fight. We barter our freedom for a power-wielding system that prides in providing us well. So they think. We were all slaves of carefully propagated consumerism, of self-created convenience till Al Gore came along and made it all pretty inconvenient. An Inconvenient Truth left us in pain, in profound regret and guilt over what we'd given away. It's this wave of sensitisation, a ripple effect of consciousness that has made the common man sit-up and take a good look around. The trees are dying, the springs are drying and the birds are songless. Earth is sick, it's in a state of crisis and lending a healing touch are filmmakers across the world by making films that are pumping levels of awareness and screaming at the top of their voices.

Starting with the home-ground, filmmaker Shekhar Kapur is already working on his script, Paani. "For those who have not heard of Irena Salina, look out for her name. She has just made a terrifying, informative, well researched documentary on the future of fresh water resources on our planet. She shows how gradually all the main water resources are being usurped by major water corporations all over the world, and how the World Bank is completely complicit. The documentary is called 'Flow"," he blogs, making this the fundamental premise of his feature, Paani. "Experts world wide, who are not living in water stressed parts of the world, are imposing the argument that " the only way to manage a dwindling resource is to get people to pay for it, so that they use it with care". Feels right in theory but what price do you set on water and whatever price you set, 85 per cent of the people will not be able to afford it!" Shekhar adds how farm houses are thirstily sucking out the ground water for private swimming pools! "Water is the new global weapon of social control and exploitation. It's a wake up call," Kapur's film is about a city set in the future facing water shortage. "It's reality of today set in the future."

Doomsday conspiracies, deadly bacteria, infected zombies, war over water, evil MNCs, rabid humans, swarms of bugs...the latest subject selling on the big screen is eco-horror and eco-thrillers. Log on to ecorazzi.com, and Hollywood filmmakers are using the fear factor. From Shyamalan's The Happenning, Will Smith's The Legend, Tom Cruise's War of the Worlds to future projects including Colony where a killer climate-change bacteria is released, Val Kilmer's The Thaw with infected woolly mammoths, Ronald Emmerich's 2012 and end of world prophecy, an abandoned radioactive city with zombies in Strays, films are taking the repercussions of global warming and climate crisis pretty seriously.

Meanwhile, there are conservationalists like On the Job's Shalini Kantayya who has been picking up environmentally relevant subjects and spinning a thought-action provoking cinema. "World Bank's Ismail Serageldin's said: if the wars of the twentieth century were fought over oil, the wars of the next century will be fought over water. I found the statistics alarming; between one-half and two-thirds of the world's population will not have access to drinking water by the year 2027. Today, there is no water running from the taps in Mumbai. Today, we used the water we stored yesterday. Suddenly, sustainability is not such an abstract concept," says Kantayya whose A Drop of Life is a story that has the power to move, inspire, and mobilize people to act on this vital issue.

Five years back John Mathan Matthew made Shikhar. No one noticed it. Syed Fayaz's documentary on mongoose changed an Act and saved this animal from being killed to make paint brushes. Green Oscar winner Mike Pandey has always fought for animal rights.

In Hollywood Goes Green Agenda of 2007, pointers have been made to focus on eco-tainment wherein producers are weaving in compelling story lines with environmental themes, assessing the impact of energy crisis and building and retrofitting studios and office buildings using recycled, non-toxic and regional construction materials, creating online media sites, social networks, music and video to engage consumers on sustainability issues, roping in sustainable fashion and the new eco-haute couture in films by using organic fibers and fabrics, choosing energy efficient products like the Vespa scooter in Steve Carrell and Anne Hathaway's "Get Smart", and going in for branding, the sustainable celebrity so the new mantra is - 'It's Hip to Be Green' where we Leonardo DiCaprio to Paris Hilton, celebrities are jumping on the environmental bandwagon. Check out Bollywood status and most of the celebs are PFA ambassadors and have gone veggie!

City's own Dr Gaurav Chhabra, in his environmental activism, has made another film, Green Warriors to save the Sector 26 pond. "It's a one of its kind place, a small wetland not even known to the oldest of residents! On the tentative list of eco tourism spots, this place is now earmarked for a VIP institute," he's all for saving this biodiversity. Are you a green warrior?

Heading: Savour this! - Indian Express
Content:
This theatre festival of socially relevant plays will reach out to the rural audiences

It's an endeavour to reach out to an audience that has limited channels of entertainment and information. Lack of infrastructure, exposure to arts, restricted funds...there are many reasons why theatre activity in villages is infrequent. To fill the gaps and build a rapport with the rural audience, the Chandigarh Sangeet Natak Akademi, along with the Cultural Affairs Department of Chandigarh Administration, is organizing at Kaimbwala a two-day theatre festival (October 11 to 12) of plays that are socially relevant. The purpose, says Kamal Tewari, is to take theatre to villages, initiate an interaction between rural and urban actors, and in spite of a lack of a well-defined cultural policy, extend theatre activity and make it a movement. "The awareness levels about art is less in rural areas and the need of the hour is to communicate with them with themes that are contemporary and relevant,'' Tewari hopes this effort will set the stage for more action and in the process, they can also encourage theatre artists from villages to come to the city with their productions. A folk theatre festival involving several places is also being thought of, as is extending this pursuit to other villages in the UT. "Tremendous work and effort in this area has been done by Gursharan Singh and one of his plays is also being staged at the festival,'' adds Kamal.

Anita Shabdeesh of Suchetak Rangmanch is a theatre director who takes numerous plays to the interiors of Punjab and feels this is an effort in the right direction. For this festival, Anita is directing Sirjana, written by Pali Bhupinder Singh and Nawan Janam by Gursharan Singh. "The former is on female foeticide, while Nawan Janam's theme is suppression of the common man. Theatre is the best way to bring about change in a subtle and effective manner and if villagers can't come to the city to see theatre, we should reach out to them, especially the women,'' feels Anita.

Nods Dr Sahib Singh, who is taking two plays written and directed by him to the festival. Anhi Gali Da Mor is a production which talks about how drug addiction is affecting our youth, "it's a problems that's rampant in Punjab and we have done innumerable shows of this,'' says Singh. In Zakhmi Khamba Di Parwaz, Sahib has Bhagat Singh, with his ideology, motivate a common man to fight the system and the play also takes up issues of unemployment, exploitation of Dalits at al. Play on.

Heading: Kart Wheels! - Indian Express
Content:
Catch the sweet and sour moments of life in Manch Tantra's 'Salt n Pepper'

The last time we met them they said their new play is about a theme that many can relate to, a press conference prior to staging of 'Salt n Pepper', team Manch Tantra reveals that the Hinglish play centres around a live-in couple. Raised eyebrows invite a deeper dig," The concept may not be popular here but there's a reason we picked up such setting. We reveal how such a couple, though in love, pull their relationship to a mess through their insecurities. As for the live-in factor it is just a fact in the play, we are not making any statements on whether it is good or bad," tells Sukriti.

What the team prides in most is that every part of their production is in-house, be it scripting, music, choreography et al. "We choose to do it all ourselves because we get to learn about the overall production," Rochak, the music composer shares that music is an essential part of their plays and "we think musically about our script." From the point of view of entertainment, "we have stepped higher on the ladder, since not only is this play a result of our maturer sensibilities but the quality especially of music is better," remarks Gautam Sharma adding that the music has been recorded in Delhi. As we get a preview of the two tracks- aasmaan main jaisa ho taara and khafa to nahin, we end up doing what the team is doing- tap our feet and smile along. The music of the play will be available at Rs 50 and a compilation of all Manch Tantra tracks may soon see the light of the day.

Catch 'Salt n Pepper' on October 10 and 11 at St Stephens School Auditorium- Sector 45, Chandigarh at 7pm.

Heading: Foot loose - Indian Express
Content:
Ritu Raj Sharma personifies Chandigarh through his sketches

I want to be Le Corbusier's second hand", a statement you wouldn't often hear in the casual ease that Ritu Raj Sharma sports. An abstract artist, Sharma has been an ardent follower of the architect. Paying a tribute to the life that Corbusier infused into the City Beautiful, Sharma has sketched the city integrating its inhabitants and landmarks. Organised by Sankhyana Environment Foundation, Himachal Pradesh, the exhibition 'Hand Creativity with Architectural Elements' showcases 20 sketches, "however I made 65 in this series," tells Sharma.

Exploring the architectural design of Chandigarh, Sharma has infused colourful portraits, sceneries, sectoral plan, the round-abouts and human figures into the compositions. Common to all sketches is the 'Open Hand'. The 'human scale' used suggestively stands for the shape of the city, "Chandigarh is resting on human scale, as the population rises, it will change the framework of the city," explains Sharma. While the most visible part of every sketch are the rectangular representations of the sectors, curves and figures also stand out in some sketches. Using bright colours like yellow, red, blue and pink against black the artist portrays the energy of the city. "The compositions and the colours tell the ideas that go on in my mind. Once I have the sheet in front of me, the lines start to take their own shape. Since I'm hoping to be the second part of Corbusier's legacy, I try to improve myself on the basis of his themes. I have seen his sketches, I hope to be as good," he signs off.

Exhibition is on at the Indus Bank Art Gallery, sector 8-C, Chandigarh till September 20 between 10am to 6pm.
