For us opening of cross-LoC trade is the revival of 60-year-old ties... and this is going to become one of the biggest CBM's," Abbasi said flanked by other members of his team. Abbasi hoped the bottlenecks in trade modalities would be removed once trade starts. "We have been assured by both countries that the hurdles will be removed with the increase in frequency and volume of trade."

The PoK trade delegation was later accorded a warm reception at the Salamabad Tourist Reception Centre by the Kashmiri traders. "We have come here to start business relations that will lay the foundation for peaceful ties that last many generations," said Muzuffarabad Traders' Federation secretary Khawaja Farooq.

Kashmir Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KCCI) president Dr Mubeen Shah termed the move an important milestone in the history of Kashmir. "For Valley traders, the start of cross-border trade would mean an important alternative for trading their wares."

Before going to Jammu, the PoK trade delegation will hold discussions with different trade bodies, especially the fruit growers. "The delegation assured us that Kashmiri items have a good market across the LoC," saud Fruit Growers' Association president Ghulam Rasool Bhat. "This visit will open new business avenues for growers here," he added.

Both countries are planning to start the trade through two points on the LoC from October 21. The Union Government has already approved a list of 23 items which can be traded, while Pakistan has sent a list of 26 items, many of them common with the Indian list.

Heading: Second blow to Jaish, ‘chief’ shot - Indian Express
Content:
There is little reason to celebrate for the Special Police Officers of Jammu and Kashmir this festive season as their salaries have not been paid for the last four months. According to official sources, the approximately 25,000 officers recruited to fight insurgency in the state have not been paid as their salaries have not been released by the Central government. Inspector General of Police, Jammu Zone K Rajendra Kumar said that, "The payment of the SPOs are made by the Central Government. However, payment of their salaries is stuck up with the Central Government and efforts by the state government are on to get their salaries released at the earliest."

Every Special Police Officer gets a fixed pay of Rs 3,000 per month at present after their salaries were revised upwards last year from the earlier Rs 1,500. The pay revision took place after the J-K Government took up the matter with the Central Government.

The Special Police Officers were recruited to help the Jammu and Kashmir Police and security forces in anti-insurgency operations in the state, sources said. They were first recruited in 1994, almost five years after the outbreak of militancy in Jammu and Kashmir. However, their job profile soon expanded to cover deployment at police stations, police posts, police out posts, and on guard duties, depending on the requirement. The SPOs deputed for anti-insurgency operations, and those deployed at police stations, police posts, police out posts, and guard duties, get full payment of Rs 3,000, while the SPOs, who are part of the Village Defence Committee (VDC) members, have to share their pay with members of the VDCs, sources said. At least two to three SPOs form part of a Village Defence Committee.Sources pointed out that there seemed little hope of their salaries being released in the near future. With Eid, Navratras and Dussehra already over and Diwali and Karva Chauth round the corner and yet no sign of their being paid, it looks set to be a damp festive season for these men and their families.

Heading: 'India will continue to build on its strong record of responsibility in n-operations' - Indian Express
Content:
Backtracking from their earlier claims, the J-K Police on Thursday admitted that they have no conclusive evidence to establish that the two suspected militants killed in a gun battle in Kupwara belonged to the southern state of Kerala.

"It is premature for us to determine their identity," Inspector General of Police (Kashmir Range) B Srinivas told reporters after a function here. "We have so far not been able to ascertain the identity of the two militants killed in Kupwara."

Srinivas said that the J-K Police were in-touch with concerned the state police to identify the slain militants. "As and when we get the information, we will give it to you (mediapersons)," he said.

The IGP added that the police had made its assumptions regarding the home state of the killed militants on the basis of various documents found on the men. "All we said was that we had recovered some literature in the Malayalam language and the identity cards from the possession of the slain militants," Srinivas said.

Based on their preliminary investigations, the J-K police had earlier claimed that the two slain militants belonged hailed from Kerala and were members of the militant outfit Lashkar-e-Toiba. The police had further revealed that an identity card was recovered from one of the dead men identified him as Shakeel Mohammad of 383 Chowk, Kovalam, Kerala.

J-K police officials had even said that they were on the lookout for three more militants from the same group who were trying to cross over to Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK). Meanwhile, the police in Kerala deny that the militants belong to their state.

Heading: Rlys eases e-ticket ID proof norm - Indian Express
Content:
At a time when his estranged nephew Raj Thackeray loses no opportunity to espouse the sons-of-the-soil cause, Shiv Sena supremo Bal Thackeray on Thursday made it clear that his son, Uddhav, was his natural successor and his party was the true champion of the "Marathi Manoos".

Making his maiden speech at the Dussehra rally, Uddhav first prostrated before the cadre. "Every time a question is asked about whom Mumbai belongs to, I tell them that if you want an answer in the Thakeri (Thackeray) language, Mumbai belongs to our father," said Uddhav. Daring critics to pose similar questions to the locals of Kolkata, Chennai and Hyderabad, he said: "There, you people are too scared to speak out, but you come to Mumbai and thumb your noses at us while asking this question."

Making it a point to emphasise that he was his father's son, he said: "Wherever I go, there is a huge crowd. A huge crowd is here also. This crowd has not collected to see Uddhav Thackeray. They are not here to listen to Uddhav Thackeray, but to listen to Uddhav Bal Thackeray."

In his customary public appearance at the party's annual Dussehra rally at the Shivaji Park grounds, Bal Thackeray said: "You have listened to Uddhav speak. People say that he speaks in a mellow way, and is not aggressive. You have heard him speak, you decide."

Making references to his advancing years, he made a pitch for supporting his son as his natural successor. "Some people are publicising as their agenda the speeches I had given earlier," he said in an oblique reference to his nephew, adding that he was an infant when the Sena was founded. "This is not something that we are doing today. The Shiv Sena was born for the Maharashtrians," he emphasised.

Without naming Raj, Uddhav said: "Those who were not good and were unfaithful left the Sena. Some of these people are speaking about their false love for the Shiv Sena chief." Raj had recently upped the ante over the Parliament privilege committee notice being sent to his uncle.

Uddhav also attacked the ruling Congress-NCP dispensation over the neglect of Mumbai, farmers suicides, and the recent communal riots in the state. He criticised Union HRD Minister Arjun Singh and Samajwadi Party leader Amar Singh over their defence of those arrested in the Jamia Nagar shootout in Delhi.

Heading: Work begins to put Garhwal mountains on railway map - Indian Express
Content:
In a move aimed to popularise e-tickets, the Indian Railways has decided to dispense with a provision that requires passengers to specify at the time of booking the proof of identification they intend to carry during the journey.

Now, a passenger booked on an e-ticket will have the choice of carrying any of the five original ID cards — voter identity card, passport, PAN card, a driving licence or photo identity cards issued by the central or state Government.

"Currently, a passenger is bound to carry the ID proof he mentions at the time of booking an e-ticket. In case the passenger forgets to carry that proof, he is considered travelling without ticket and penalised accordingly, even if he has some other valid proof to establish his identity. This has become a cause of complaint and is acting as an impediment in the proliferation of e-ticketing and has prompted a change in policy," a senior ministry official said.

"However, it will be the responsibility of the passenger carrying proof of identification that other passengers booked on the e-sticket are bonafide passengers and are not travelling in someone else's name," the official said adding that in case none of the passengers were carrying any one of the prescribed proofs of identity, they would be treated as travelling without ticket and charged accordingly.

Heading: UPA may ask Orissa for Bajrang Dal dossier, looking at Governor’s report - Indian Express
Content:
Kicking off an ambitious project to link the Garhwal mountains with a rail network, the Indian Railways has resumed work on a feasibility survey for laying a rail track along the 126-km Rishikesh-Karan Prayag stretch.

According to Divisional Railway Manager (DRM) Moradabad Onkar Singh, almost 80 per cent of the survey had been completed in the year 2000 and the current process of updating it was underway. Talking to The Indian Express, he said, "There is not much economic activity on this stretch. But at the same time there are lots of tourists coming to the region. Once the broad guage track is laid, there will be an all-round improvement in the economic activity in the area."

Almost 30 lakh pilgrims visit Kedar Nath, Badri Nath and Hemkunth Sahib annually besides those who visit other tourist destinations of Uttarakhand. Setting up of a railway line in this area will benefit Dehradun, Rishikesh, Pauri, Tehri, Rudraprayag, Chamoli and Hardwar.

Singh also said a survey of the proposed Dehradun-Kalsi railway track was almost complete and the Railway Board was expected to grant its approval to the project soon. This project envisages laying of a railway track on the 50-km stretch between Dehradun and Kalsi via Nayagaon and Rampur. Meanwhile, a proposal to lay a double track between Dehradun and Laksar has also been sent to the Railway Board.

Heading: ‘What if I say he tried to rape me, I killed him... might save us’ - Indian Express
Content:
With some key allies demanding a ban on the Bajrang Dal for its alleged role in violence against Christians in Orissa, the UPA government plans to seek a detailed report from the Naveen Patnaik government on the activities of the outfit in the state.

Sources in Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) told The Indian Express that data relating to the alleged involvement of the Bajrang Dal in fomenting communal violence has already been collected from other states. "But so far, there is no decision to recommend a ban on the outfit. Any decision in this regard will be taken after scrutinising whatever details we get from Orissa and various agencies," a senior official said.

The UPA is divided over the issue of banning the Bajrang Dal. While key allies like Lalu Prasad Yadav and Ramvilas Paswan are all for an immediate ban, others, some senior Congress ministers included, maintain that a ban is possible only if there is adequate evidence that can stand legal scrutiny.

At the Cabinet meeting yesterday, Home Minister Shivraj Patil said his ministry had collected some evidence against the Bajrang Dal but more evidence was needed to firm up a case for a ban.

Sources said the Centre is also looking at a report sent by Orissa Governor Murlidhar Chandrakant Bhandare to the President.

In his report, which mainly refers to the violence against Christians in the state, the Governor is said to have mentioned the involvement of the Bajrang Dal in the hate campaign. The President has forwarded the report to the MHA for appropriate action.

Heading: Let’s Also sell uranium to India: Aussie oppn to govt - Indian Express
Content:
Small-time Kannada actresss Maria Monica Susairaj apparently plans to retract her statement on the murder of TV executive Neeraj Grover, for which she wants her boyfriend and co-accused Emile Jerome Mathew's help — so that they can both "save their lives".

In a long, at times intimate, letter written to Mathew from her Byculla prison cell three weeks ago, Susairaj said her statement— that it was Mathew who killed Grover and she only helped him dispose of the body — had been extracted under duress, and she now wanted to confess she knifed Grover to death after he tried to rape her.

Susairaj, 27, and Mathew, 25, originally from Mysore, were arrested on May 21 for the murder of Grover, 25, a top executive at Synergy Adlabs and a former creative head at Balaji Telefilms. Police said Mathew had stabbed Grover after he arrived at Susairaj's rented apartment in Mumbai and found Grover naked in her bedroom.

The couple allegedly cut the body into small pieces, stuffed them into three bags and, dumping the bags in the countryside, set them on fire.

Despite Susairaj's statement that she was party only to the destruction of evidence, the police in June named her as the main accused who had engineered the crime. Mathew is currently lodged in Arthur Road prison.

The Indian Express is in possession of a copy of the six-page letter that Susairaj wrote over September 19 and September 20. It is in Kannada, interspersed with English words and sentences. According to prison rules, prisoners are allowed to write letters, which after vetting by prison authorities, are sent forward to the addressee.

The superintendent of Byculla prison, Sudhir Kingre, confirmed the letter is genuine.

In the letter, Susairaj tells Mathew that she has been studying legal books and case laws related to self-defence during rape attempts. "I just read one case law. The father of a child killed a man to protect his daughter from being raped to defend his daughter, he killed. The Supreme Court had set aside his conviction, refer Section 96, 97, 100 of IPC," she writes.

"What if I say that night he forced me physically and tried to rape me by threatening me with a knife. When he kept the knife aside, I took it and in self-defence, panicked and stabbed him," Susairaj says. She adds that to "save" her, Mathew had helped destroy the body the next morning after arriving from Kochi. "My head and chest hurts a lot when I have to say or think or write that I was the one who killed him. But this way, we can both save our lives and I am ready for this, darling."

Susairaj repeatedly tells Mathew, who was a classmate of her younger sister in Mysore before joining the Navy, how much she loved him, but how things had gone wrong between them. "You lied to me so much, but I was still very loving and caring. If you had not lied to me, I would not have lied to you, darling. And if I hadn't lied, you wouldn't have killed him."

Susairaj's lawyer G S Kunnur said he did not know about the letter. "If Maria has actually written the letter then it might be an attempt by her to clear doubts created in Emile's mind after her confession," he said. He added that she may not be able to retract her confession now, since much time has been lost.

Mathew's lawyer Raja Thakur also said he was not aware of the letter, since Mathew did not discuss his personal life with him.

"If you are to be believed, then it shows how sharp a mind Maria has. First she confesses and puts the entire blame on Emile and now after her realisation that she won't go scot-free, she is resorting to such tricks," he told The Indian Express.

Heading: End of debate: Govt shifts focus from emissions to mileage - Indian Express
Content: Australian opposition parties on Thursday pressed the federal government to review its stand not to sell uranium to India, saying that with New Delhi back in the nuclear club, the current "hypocritical" policy will only hurt mining companies.The opposition parties said the government did not object to the NSG waiver for India. "Now that the US-India agreement has been made law, the Rudd government is in an untenable position by refusing to allow the sale of Australian uranium to India under the same terms, conditions and IAEA inspection program as Australian uranium sales to China," said opposition resources spokesman Ian Macfarlane.

Heading: Bush signs deal into law, guarantees India fuel supply, reprocessing rights - Indian Express
Content:
Automakers may soon be forced to reveal exactly how many kilometres their vehicles run on a litre of fuel. Last week, the government finally decided to override the long-standing objections to the proposed fuel efficiency-based regulatory regime — shifting focus from regulating vehicular emissions to regulating vehicle mileage.

Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister T K A Nair revealed the government's line at a meeting of all major stakeholders on October 3, sources said. A committee is likely to be formed soon to decide on the exact methodology of fixing mileage-based fuel efficiency norms, and identify the nodal agency for its implementation.

"It has been clearly stated and accepted now by the government that fuel economy standards in terms of mileage— kilometres per litre of fuel consume— must be introduced as part of India's fuel efficiency norms," a top official told The Indian Express."The decision is consistent with India's line on the impact of carbon emissions on climate change. The idea is to save on energy resources through fuel-efficient vehicles rather than trying to directly reduce carbon dioxide emissions. This is the practice in most developed countries like the US, Canada and Japan," the official said.

The decision brings closure to an old disagreement on the issue. While automakers have been resisting the introduction of a system that would make closely guarded mileage figures public in a highly price- and mileage-sensitive market, the government itself has been divided.

The Ministry of Shipping, Road Transport & Highways and the Ministry of Heavy Industry have been opposing the mileage-based energy-efficiency regime. The Ministry of Power and the Ministry of Environment and Forests have, on the other hand, been arguing in its favour.

In August, the Standing Committee on Emissions formed by the Ministry of Shipping, Road Transport & Highways recommended fuel efficiency norms based on carbon dioxide emissions similar to Euro/Bharat standards currently in use.

The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) under the Ministry of Power took the other view: recommending that vehicles should be classified from '1 star' to '5 stars' based on their fuel economy in kilometres per litre, with a minimum mileage of 10 km per litre earning 1 star. The BEE suggested that labeling be initially kept voluntary for the automobile industry but subsequently made mandatory.

The power ministry has been arguing that fuel efficiency and carbon emission norms should be viewed separately. The Ministry of Environment & Forests has said that fuel efficiency or emissions norms based on carbon dioxide "would not be acceptable", and India's "approach on carbon emissions in the climate change negotiations" must be kept in mind before any decision is taken.

India's National Action Plan on Climate Change, unveiled in June 2008, articulates an energy security-based approach, which has as ancillary benefit a reduction in greenhouse gases. Instead of directly reducing greenhouse gas emissions, India is committed more to energy security and fuel saving.

Anumita Roy Choudhary of the Centre for Science & Environment described the government's move as "very welcome" and "long-awaited".

"Emission norms like Bharat III etc control the quantum of emissions, but India has no fuel efficiency standards at all in terms of how much fuel vehicles are consuming per kilometer," she said. "India is seeing a motorisation explosion... by 2030 we will be importing 86% of our crude oil needs, so it is essential to introduce fuel efficiency standards."

Heading: Modasa: Gujarat police deny probe bias, say 60 Hindus are among 150 questioned - Indian Express
Content:
More than three years after the blueprint was outlined in a Indo-US joint statement in Washington, the nuclear deal got its final legal sanctity today when US President George W Bush signed the 123 agreement into law and made it clear that US will fulfill all its fuel assurance commitments in the agreement. He also specified that the agreement recognises India's right to reprocess spent fuel.

External Affairs Minister Pranab Mukherjee and

Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice will formally ink the deal tomorrow.

In an effort to address any doubts in India over the contents of the legislation he was signing and concerns that it had deviated from what the two countries had negotiated, Bush recorded in his signing statement, which is a reflection of how the US President interprets a particular law for further implementation and has its own sanctity, that Washington will meet all its obligations in the 123 agreement.

"This legislation is important as it enables me to bring the 123 agreement into force and to accept on behalf of the United States the obligations contained in the agreement," he stated.

India had raised certain concerns in the Bill passed by the US Congress. These related to certain aspects in the introductory section of the Bill, where it was specified that India's safeguarded fuel reserve should be "commensurate with reasonable reactor requirements".

This was contrary to the 123 agreement where US had agreed to let India store lifetime supplies of fuel for its reactors. Indian officials pointed out this inconsistency during Prime Minister Manmohan Singh's recently concluded visit to Washington. Bush had assured Singh that Washington would ensure that what is finally signed is to New Delhi's satisfaction.

So, in his signing statement, the US President stated: "In addition, the legislation does not change the fuel assurance commitments that the US government has made to the Government of India, as recorded in the 123 agreement."

The other key issue was the Congress's intention to maintain tighter oversight on India's reprocessing activities. To this end, the Bill contains a right of disapproval for the Congress on a future Indo-US agreement to trade in enrichment and reprocessing technologies. This was, in fact, the most important sticking point for House International Relations Committee Chairman Howard Berman who wanted to the bind the US President to inform the US Congress at least 15 days before starting negotiations on any such agreement in the future.

He withdrew this clause after Rice spoke to him and underlined US commitment to limiting trade in ENR technologies. However, the legislation still requires any such agreement with India to lie in Congress for more time than the Atomic Energy Act, otherwise, specifies.

The added complexity prompted India to ask US to clarify matters when the legislation is finally signed into law as the 123 agreement clearly recognises India's right to reprocess and does not foreclose the possibility of an agreement between both countries on ENR trade in the future. Here again, Bush was not short giving that clarification today.

"The agreement grants India advance consent to reprocessing which will be brought into effect upon conclusion of arrangements and procedures of a dedicated reprocessing facility under IAEA safeguards," he recorded in his signing statement. The language, incidentally, is quite similar to what is mentioned in the 123 agreement. Indian Ambassador to US Ronen Sen, in fact, went on record after the signing ceremony in the White House that all concerns had been adequately addressed. "Absolutely," he remarked when asked if the President's address at the signing of the legislation met all of India's concerns.

"I think the statement (of Bush) speaks for itself... all concerns that have been expressed, who fear the implications of certain elements of the legislation, all those have been met," Sen said in response to a query on fuel supply assurances.

Heading: Successful monsoon promises rabi riches in Doon valley - Indian Express
Content:
More than 60 of the nearly 150 people questioned in connection with the September 29 blast in Modasa town of Sabarkantha district were Hindus, Gujarat police officials investigating the case said.

The bomb, hidden in a motorcycle parked near a mosque, exploded three days before Eid, killing a 15-year-old boy and leaving several injured.

Under fire from Muslim leaders for bringing only their community under the scanner — Congress MP Madhusudan Mistry even alleged that the focus of the probe appeared to be part of a politically-motivated exercise — police said they were examining both Hindus and Muslims for possible leads.

Dy SP K K Mysorewala told The Indian Express: "We have so far questioned nearly 150 people. Of this, more than 60 are Hindus living in localities in and around the town." He said they had no specific lead so far. "We are not ruling out the possibility of non-Muslims being behind the blast but we have no evidence yet. We have detained and questioned suspects, without prejudice, irrespective of religion."

The engine number of the motorcycle in which the bomb was placed had been completely erased, the etchings filed away. But it appears that the chassis number had only been tampered with, some numbers overwritten. Police say they are counting on forensics to decipher the original chassis number to get to the owner.

Heading: Winds of change - Indian Express
Content:
Agriculturists in the Doon Valley have plenty to celebrate this year. With the entire belt receiving exceptionally well-distributed rains during the monsoon season, the forecast for the next rabi (winter) crop is very encouraging.

A former senior official from the Indian Council for Agricultural Research (ICAR), Gobind Ballabh Raturi, told The Indian Express, "Farmers in the Doon Valley can look forward to a good rabi crop. Thanks to the successful monsoon, the region is likely to witness good mustard, wheat and vegetable crops over the next few months."

The Doon Valley is known for its high-yielding agricultural belt, starting from Vikasnagar in the north to Rishikesh in the south. The rabi crops that are grown here include wheat, mustard and vegetables, with peas being the most important cash crop.

The director of the Meteorological Department in Dehradun, Dr Anand Sharma says, "The most interesting feature of this year's monsoon has been that the rains were well spread. The distribution was very good. During the months of June, July and September, there was good rainfall every week. Despite there being a slight lull in September, the Valley did receive rains and a small Western Disturbance is likely to bring showers till October 9." He added that the moisture levels in the soil are very high, making it ideal for sowing the rabi crop.

Giving details about the rainfall pattern, Dr Sharma disclosed that during this monsoon season, stretching from June to September, the Doon valley has received 2,240 mm of rainfall. The average figure for the state of Uttarakhand stood at 1,199 mm.

Although the region has been experiencing a similar quantity of rainfall in previous years as well, this year saw an exceptionally good distribution with barely a day passing without some area receiving rain showers.

This has also led to the present kharif crop, which is to be harvested from the end of October onwards, being in very good shape. In terms of the kharif crop, the region is well known for its high production of sugarcane and paddy. The rains this year have ensured that there was no need for the farmers to irrigate their fields. "The soil was saturated and there was no water stress. The farmers did not have to spend on electricity and labour to irrigate their fields," said Dr Sharma.

He further pointed out that the continuing cloud cover in the month of October might lead to some damage to the paddy crop in certain places due to blast fungus, but the problem can be curbed if farmers monitor their crops carefully and spray fungicide after the Western Disturbance moves away. He suggested that the sprays may only be resorted to if the disease is exceeding the economic threshold value of the crop.

Heading: Agriculture losing ground to service sector in J&K - Indian Express
Content:
For a state whose total contribution of rice to the central pool is nearly 50 per cent, diversification from paddy does not seem to be happening anytime in the near future. A good minimum support price (MSP) has seen the area under paddy cultivation go up by almost 50,000 hectares in Punjab this year while that under other kharif crops such as cotton and sugarcane has reduced.

Though diversification still seems a long way off, it's not just another paddy season for Punjab. The state has been proactive in enforcing some stern measures including something it had never done before — reining in its errant rice millers.

To begin with, the ban on sowing of water-guzzling paddy before June 10 was enforced to arrest the state's fast-depleting water table. While early rains this year were a windfall for the water table, the state was saved from two crops of the early maturity varieties, sown as early as May, when the monsoons are still a good two months away.

Another favourable development in this regard, albeit unintentional, was the area under basmati varieties registering a huge leap — of nearly one lakh hectares this year. These late-sowing varieties (sown only after the monsoon sets in) also proved to be good news for the state's depleting water table.

Meanwhile, a labour shortage and the consequent rise in wages saw another first — large-scale mechanical cultivation of paddy this year. Since the cost of operating the paddy transplanters (Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 per acre) was much lower as compared to the prevailing labour costs (Rs 1,200-1,800 an acre), many farmers opted for this more predictable and economical option. Also, the Chinese ones came for just Rs 1.65 lakh.

To give the much-needed policy push, the government is approaching manufacturers of combine harvesters to make paddy transplanters and also intends to import some for making them available to farmers through the cooperative system of kisan kendras besides providing subsidy to those who buy them.

"New techniques such as direct seeding and transplantation on ridges were also started this year and led to distinct improvement in yield," says the Punjab Farmers Commission.

And since no task well begun is creditable if it does not end well, Punjab, for the first time in its rice milling history, took on the powerful lobby of its 3000-odd rice millers this year.

Its 2008-09 kharif policy for paddy laid down stern condition that custom milling (milling of paddy for central pool) will be allowed subject to payment of penalty by the defaulting mills, which did not supply rice to the FCI after receiving paddy from the procurement agencies.

In addition to penalty, the defaulters have also to tide over the gap of levy rice (rice milled for their own business). And millers are not taking any chances. "Against the total penalty of Rs 8 crore, we have already received more than 50 per cent (Rs 5 crore) from defaulters. Though done for the first time, our condition of not permitting custom milling of paddy till they made good the penalty and levy gap has worked. This would go a long way and we expect not a single rice mill to default on timely delivery of rice next year," says Director, Punjab Food and Supply Department S P Singh.

Heading: Flower Power - Indian Express
Content:
In a situation mirroring the change in the national economy, the tertiary sector in Jammu and Kashmir is fast threatening to overtake the primary sector. Agriculture, once the mainstay of the economy, is being increasingly abandoned by people in favour of jobs in the private sector leading to a marked slump in the primary sector in the last few years.

As per official figures, the contribution of the primary sector, which includes forestry, livestock and agricultural sector, to the State Domestic Product has witnessed a decline between 2001 and 2007.

The year 2001 saw a contribution of 31.4 per cent by the primary sector, which declined to 30 per cent in 2002. Though 2003 saw a marginal rise to 31per cent, it stagnated at 30 per cent in 2004 and 2005 and dipped to 29 per cent in 2006. In 2006-07, while the contribution of the primary sector to the state's economy remained 29 per cent, the secondary sector contributed 24 per cent and the tertiary sector 46 per cent.

Officials attribute this decrease to the growing urbanisation of J&K. They added that even though the actual growth rate of agriculture in the state had shown a consistent increase, it had lagged behind the national average. The rate has been 5.13 per cent in 2002-03, 5.17 per cent in 2003-04, 5.23 per cent in 2004-05, 5.73 per cent in 2005-06 and 6 per cent in 2006-07. The annual growth rate has been 5.45 per cent. However, at the national level the actual growth rate has been 3.8 per cent in 2002-03, 8.5 per cent in 2003-04, 7.5 percent in 2004-05, 9 percent in 2005-06 and 9.2 per cent in 2006-07.

Officials further reveal that there has been a remarkable shift in the economy in favour of the tertiary sector and the contribution of the primary sector has declined from 56.64 per cent in 1970 at constant prices to 31 per cent in 2006-07. The corresponding contribution of the tertiary sector has increased from 28 percent to 46 per cent.

Heading: Hello - Indian Express
Content:
After setting up Asia's biggest tulip garden on the foothills of Zabarwan forest range close to Dal Lake, the state's Floriculture department is now thinking of exporting the flower in a big way.

The government, too, is pitching in with a cold storage facility set to come up on the city outskirts.

"At present, we are storing flower saplings and ornamental plants in polythene shelters," said Director, Floriculture, Dr Sarwar Naqash.

"It's a temporary arrangement and makes the flowers vulnerable to drying. The cold storage will go a long way in preserving the flowers and thus help in their export."

Principal Secretary, Agriculture and Floriculture, Sonali Kumar said Srinagar will "very soon" have a big cold storage for flowers.

"This will give a boost to the floriculture sector and commercial farming of ornamental flowers."

"Farmers are encouraged to grow flowers and ornamental plants on a large scale given their rising demand not only in the country but outside as well. Besides, climatic conditions of the Valley are favourable for their growth," she said.

"Last year, we imported some 10 lakh tulips of 15 varieties from Holland. Next year onwards, however, we will have large quantities of tulips available with us, which we would send to different states and also export aboard," he said.

There is a huge demand for flowers during winter, especially in European countries.

Officials said flowers couldn't be exported earlier due to absence of a cold storage facility. "But with the cold storage being built now, we have already chalked plans for export of flowers," said Naqash.

The Floriculture department, which was brought under the commercial sector two years ago, has enlisted 540 flower growers. The number is expected to increase.

"The registered beneficiaries are being provided technical counselling by the experts of the department," said Naqash. "Time will come when, like fruits and vegetables, flowers, too, will become a big trade in Kashmir."

Growers, too, seem to have understood the commercial value of flowers. "Earlier, I used to sell different kinds of flowers grown in my farm within the state only. Now, I am looking forward to expanding my business beyond the state's borders. I will also export some varieties," said Md Maqbool, of north Kashmir.

Heading: Sourav Ganguly must go out as a man at peace with himself - Indian Express
Content:
Cast: Sharman Joshi, Sohail Khan, Gul Panag, Amrita Arora, Isha Koppikar, Sharat Saxena, Dalip Tahil, Salman Khan, Katrina Kaif

Director: Atul Agnihotri

One night in a call centre, there comes a phone call. Really, a phone call in a call centre, cries Salman Khan (playing himself), in mock amazement. Pretty laptop-toting story-teller (Katrina) smiles mysteriously, and begins her yarn. And as yarns go, it isn't too bad. The trouble with 'Hello', based on Chetan Bhagat's mega-seller, is that isn't too good either.

It's a dark rainy night, and Shyam aka Sam ( Sharman) is hurting because the love of his life Priyanka ( Gul) has said yes to a rich NRI. Varun aka Vrroom (Sohail) has his eye on Esha ( Isha), but all she wants is to become a model. Radhika (Amrita) tries to please her horrible mom-in-law by day, and pops anti-depressants by night because her husband is a two-timing cad. And Military Uncle (Sharat) is upset because his US-based son wants to have nothing to do with him.

These sad sack call centre agents rattle around in a large room with work stations placed miles apart. That's a total wrong number. Except for a barmy systems guy, and smarmy boss (Dalip), there doesn't seem to be a soul else in Atul Agnihotri's scheme of things: he's clearly not aware of all those rows and rows of super-busy souls-- sitting elbow-to-elbow, nattering the night away on their headphones and mikes-- that seem to be more the norm in these nocturnal work hives echoing with faux American accents.

You could also call 'Hello' a case of six characters in search of a zingy script. Bhagat's novel is not literature, but manages to capture some of the hurly-hurly of New India's preoccupation with instant money, getting ahead and greenbacks. The film's canvas is largely empty, so the good turn by Sharman Joshi gets lost. As does some genuinely funny banter, and the Khan family's full turn-out (Salman with his shirt off, girl-friend Kat in a cameo, `chota bhai' Arbaaz in a walk on) on account of Agnihotri being the Khans' brother-in-law.

Even that thing that call centre types are allegedly indulging in all the time—making out on down-time in the back of convenient SUVs —pictured here on Sharman and Gul, lacks fire. It's tepid, just like the movie.

Heading: ‘Seniors shouldn’t quit in a bunch’ - Indian Express
Content:
Sourav Ganguly isn't finished with the game yet; he has merely announced that he will retire a month from now. And so till he walks off the ground for the last time he, and more important all of us, need to look ahead. It's been a fine career but it isn't over yet and looking back at it while there is still a peak to conquer isn't very clever .

Given all the hype, itself a part of life in India now, the platitudes that have come his way, and the anger he has apparently expressed in a Bengali newspaper, it is critical that he scores runs quickly in the series. If he doesn't score enough, Indian audiences can move very quickly from being fans to being caustic. The last thing a player wants is to stay on in the side merely because of sentiment even if it weakens the side.

That is why I find it a little difficult to follow what the new chairman of selectors has said. Srikkanth suggested that Ganguly could now bat freely and without the sword dangling over him which, when he was a player, he didn't like either. I believe, quite to the contrary, that Ganguly has pulled a fair bit of pressure towards himself. Also, don't forget he is not guaranteed four Test matches because nobody can make deals like that.

But having known Ganguly over the years, I suspect he won't mind the pressure too much because if he delivers now, having upped the stakes so much, his legend will only grow. All good players back themselves and so has he. There is another reason I would like him to score runs here. A lot of very fine players retire as bitter men; for the rest of their substantial life they carry the hurt of denial, believing they could have done more. It is one of the saddest things in the game and given the kind of career he has had, Ganguly must go out as a man at peace with himself.

Luckily, unlike financial institutions, the retirement of cricketers doesn't have a ripple effect. I am not surprised at all that Anil Kumble was unhappy (most would have angry!) at the suggestion that he was moving on too. All he had said was that this was his last chance to beat Australia and you can't argue with that because the next test series is two and a half years away. The probability of him playing till then is as strong as the chance of peace in Afghanistan.

But Kumble has a point. And a reason to be upset. India and Australia have produced consistently outstanding test cricket since that great series of 2001. This is one of the highlights of the cricket calendar and yet, the focus is not on performance but on when great players are going to leave, presumably on the assumption that they are no longer good enough. Kumble has always said that he is now taking his career series by series and for a man who has rarely demonstrated anything but dignity, I think we should take his word for it and move on.

Curiously though, this has had a positive side-effect (doesn't some good come out of everything? Or is that only in our movies?); for the first time there has been no mention of Sachin Tendulkar. A man who stood apart has now been herded into a group and collectively dissected. He won't mind that too much for he is at heart a simple man who likes to go about things quietly, in his own way. Now, he won't be thinking about retirement just yet! I suspect it will be a joint rather than a bowler that will cause that decision to be taken!

So a fine series gets underway with a fine player proving that statistics of the past rarely have relevance to the present. If we could predict what cricketers are likely to do based on what they have done in the past, this wouldn't be the greatest game in the world. Ricky Ponting struggled initially but good players get over small phases in their innings like a mountaineer does the loss of a water bottle on the way. When the captain is in a good mood, it rubs off on the others and Ponting will have gone to bed in a very good mood.

Heading: New Zealand upset by new Bangladesh - Indian Express
Content:
With Sachin Tendulkar just 77 runs short of taking over from him as the highest scorer in Test cricket, former West Indies captain Brian Lara, in the city en route to Australia, wished his "good friend" luck, and hoped that he would get there in the first Test itself. With all the talk in India revolving around seniors and retirement plans, Lara, who will not be playing in the ICL this season, said it was important that the phasing out was gradual. Excerpts from an interview:

On Sourav Ganguly's retirement

•I think any sportsman would like to go out on his terms. Sourav is a great servant of Indian cricket and has proved to be a great leader, especially away from home. I remember the series against Australia (2003) where his innings helped India draw at the Gabba. He has been a catalyst for change and upward mobility for Indian cricket. Any great player leaving will leave a gap but that also means an opportunity for a youngster.

On whether it's time for other seniors to go

• I think it should be a gradual process. You don't want the top five players going at the same time. It happened with us in the early 90s, when we lost Viv Richards, Gordon Greenidge and Malcolm Marshall, and I don't want this to happen to Indian cricket. India should be very careful about who goes — and when. I understand they want young blood but you don't want to expose them all at the same time.

On whether the board should have any right to negotiate players' retirement

• Every player wants to retire on a high. I think every player deserves to go out when he wants and not when the board or selectors want. They have been performing for such a long time, it would be unfair for someone else to tell them when they should quit.

On if India are favourites in this series

• You cannot take anything away from Australia. They are still the number one. What I do know is that they aren't as strong as they were 3-4 years ago. But you cannot take them lightly.

On whether India-Australia clashes are becoming bigger than the Ashes

• The Border-Gavaskar Trophy is surely very huge but it will be wrong to compare it to the Ashes, that has a lot of history.

On Sachin closing in on his record for most Test runs

• I wish Sachin all the very best. I hope he breaks it in Bangalore itself and continues scoring runs the way he's done throughout his career. I feel very proud to be in the same league as Gavaskar, Border and Tendulkar. We all have to appreciate what he has done. He is one of the greatest to have played the game.

On who he sees getting past Tendulkar

• Ricky (Ponting) is a class player. I feel he is the only player currently who can break Sachin's record in the future.

Lara no longer with ICL

Brian Lara has confirmed he won't be part of the ICL. "If I'm heading to Australia, then how can I be with the ICL," asked Lara. ICL officials also confirmed Lara would not be a part of the league anymore. Last ICL season, there had been enough rumours about Lara wanting to opt out of the rebel league but being forced to stick to his commitments. The second edition of ICL is scheduled to begin on Friday. Asked if he would be opting for IPL, Lara said "I don't want to go much about ICL or IPL. Both are good for the game."

Heading: Two Tests cancelled to give Lankan cricketers IPL break - Indian Express
Content:
Zunaed Siddique and Mashrafe Mortaza scripted Bangladesh's first-ever victory over New Zealand in one-day cricket with a comfortable seven-wicket win in the opening match here on Thursday. The only other time Bangladesh had beaten New Zealand was during a warm-up game before the 2007 World Cup.

Left-hander Siddique scored a brilliant 85 for his maiden half-century to anchor his team's successful chase of a 202-run target in 45.3 overs at the Sher-e-Bangla National Stadium, after paceman Mortaza took four for 44 to jolt the tourists.

Skipper Mohammad Ashraful notched an unbeaten 60 to guide Bangladesh to their first win over the Black Caps in 12 one-dayers, as he and Siddique added 109 for the third wicket to upset their formidable opponents.

Ashraful was full of praise for his team's effort after the match. "I am elated that it's the first win against New Zealand and first against a major country under my captaincy," said Ashraful, who took over last year.

Mortaza and left-arm spinner Abdur Razzak (three for 32) set up the win by restricting New Zealand to 201 for nine in their 50 overs. Jacob Oram top-scored with a solid 57 and added 70 runs for the seventh wicket with Vettori (30), but that was not enough for New Zealand to avoid their lowest one-day total against the hosts. Their previous lowest was 224 at Chittagong in 2004.

Bangladesh lost opener Tamim Iqbal (12) early but Siddique and Mushfiqur Rahim (30) added 67 for the second wicket before Ashraful sealed the fate of the match. Siddique hit eight boundaries during his 139-ball knock while Ashraful hit five boundaries and a six in his rapid 56-ball innings.

Earlier, Mortaza jolted the New Zealand top order after Bangladesh won the toss and elected to field. He was brilliantly supported by Razzak as both grabbed five of the first six wickets to fall after New Zealand raced to a solid start of 47 through Jesse Ryder (34) and Brendon McCullum (14).

Mortaza dismissed Ryder and Jamie How in his first spell and returned to dismiss Kyle Mills, while Razzak kept the pressure up by dismissing Scott Styris and Daniel Flynn.

Heading: ‘Rebel’ ICL gets ready for second innings - Indian Express
Content:
The controversy over the release of Sri Lanka players for next year's Indian Premier League, which clashes with their England tour, was resolved on Thursday with the SLC permitting them to participate in the Twenty20 tournament.

"It has been decided to release the players for next year's IPL and send a full strength Sri Lankan team to England for one-dayers beginning on May 27, 2009," a top SLC source said on Thursday. The IPL is scheduled from April 10 to May 25. "The proposed two-Test series against England that was to be part of the tour will be cancelled but this is subject to approval by the ECB," the source added.

This followed a recent meeting between IPL chairman Lalit Modi and Sri Lanka Players' Association secretary Graeme Labrooy. Twelve Lankan players are contracted with IPL franchises.

India has also agreed to resume a tri-nation tournament involving India, South Africa and Sri Lanka in 2009 and in Sri Lanka in 2010. The BCCI has also agreed to include Sri Lanka for a tri-nation ODI tournament during Pakistan's Test series in India early next year.

The Champions Twenty20 League has also agreed to pay $40 million to Sri Lanka Cricket for sending its team for league matches for the next 10 years, to make up for the guarantee money SLC will forfeit due to cancellation of the England Tests.

SLC Chairman Arjuna Ranatunga had insisted on these funds for development of domestic cricket in Sri Lanka before reaching a compromise.

Heading: Now, Singapore gets its own Pravasi Divas - Indian Express
Content:
The city is bustling with nervous energy and unseasonal rains have added to the mystery ahead of the second season of the Indian Cricket League (ICL), which begins on Friday at the Lal Bahadur Shastri Stadium. Hyderabad will also host the finals.

Most of the players were locked up in their hotels rooms as the rains refused to relent, and some hit the gym. But then, there is always uncertainty around the league, branded a 'rebel' by the Indian board.

It could either swim with the T20 tide, or get swept away by the BCCI-backed Indian Premier League, and the next month will provide clues as to whether it was worth taking on the establishment.

"We hope to raise the quality of the championship. Indians now love their T20 and with the players in ICL having adapted to the format, will provide you with all the entertainment, " said Chris Harris, the skipper of defending champions Hyderabad Heroes.

On his team's chances in the opener against the Lahore Badshahs, Harris said: "They're a tough side but we would like to carry forward our performance of last year." The Hyderabad team had beaten Inzamam-ul Haq's Lahore in a bowl-out and the former Pakistan skipper is eager to settle scores.

"This time we have some scores to settle. We'll be geared up for our first game," Inzamam said.

Much like the IPL opening in April this year, the ICL is planning a start-studded show before the match, with a performance by Shiamak Davar's dance troupe and with Rakhi Sawant the chief of Zeebras, the ICL cheerleading group.

The ICL has announced a prize money corpus of Rs.13.72 crore for the tournament, with a winners' purse of Rs. 2 crore. Each Man of the Match award will be worth Rs 2 lakhs and the Man of the Series will get Rs 40 lakhs.

The tournament, ending on November 16, will be played in Hyderabad, Panchkula, Ahmedabad and Gurgaon.

Heading: Ponting breaks India jinx - Indian Express
Content:
In an effort to reach out to the the Indian diaspora in Singapore and the Asia-Pacific, a two-day international conference modelled on India's annual Pravasi Bhartiya Divas was inaugurated in Singapore on Thursday. Entitled "PBD Singapore — Towards a Dynamic Indian Diaspora", the conference is being organised by the Singapore Indian Chamber of Commerce & Industry (SICCI), the Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs (MOIA) and the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII).

Inaugurating the conference, expected to be attended by over 800 delegates from 20 countries, India's Minister of Overseas Affairs Vayalar Ravi said that the mini-PBD was a concrete step towards connecting "India with the rest of India settled across the world."

With bilateral trade ties between India and Singapore on the rise and expected to be to the tune of 18 billion, Ravi added that the event was an outcome of Prime Minister Manmohan Singh's decision to create an Overseas Affairs Ministry to leverage the strength of the Indian diaspora spread across 110 countries. While Singapore Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong will deliver the inaugural keynote address on Friday, India's Science and Technology Minister Kapil Sibal and Ravi are among the key speakers from India.

"The Overseas Ministry was the brainchild of Dr Manmohan Singh as he realised the importance and the contributions of Non Resident Indians (NRI's) during the financial crisis of the 90's and the response to the huge turnout of delegates that mainly include diplomats and politicians of both the countries is very encouraging," the Minister said.

Reffering to Singapore's strategic location between India and the rest of the Pacific-Asian countries, Singapore Deputy Prime Minister S Jaykumar said that Singapore was a springboard for India to reach out to other countries. "Nearly nine per cent of the population in Singapore is of Indian origin. We have a great past to share and with Indian nationals coming to work in this country as professionals, students and even for leisure, there is great potential to build ties with our young nation which is uniquely aware of it's cultural diversity," he said adding that over 3,000 Indian companies are registered in Singapore currently.

With global markets reeling under the onslaught of the US financial meltdown, Indian High Commissioner Dr S Jaishankar said that Singapore was considerably less affected because of the presence of growing economies like India and China. The next PBD will be organised in Chennai in January 2009.

Heading: Symonds will have to prove himself to make comeback: Sutherland - Indian Express
Content:
Had tennis great Pete Sampras gotten over his clay-phobia and won the French Open, he might have known how Ricky Ponting was feeling on Thursday. Despite an overall away average of 52, and a world record of maximum tons on foreign soil, the brownish carpets in India have repeatedly exposed Ponting's weakness. But on Thursday at the Chinnaswamy Stadium, the Aussie captain changed the world's perception of his batting with a flawless innings of 123 to wipe out the only smudge on his glowing whites.

In the morning, when he walked in after opener Matthew Hayden was dismissed off the third delivery, retribution must have been the last thing on Ponting's mind. A batsman with an average of 12 from eights Tests can't afford the aggressive stance of vendetta, and he was expectedly circumspect with Ishant Sharma in the middle of an inspired spell. Ponting's typical early tentativeness — showcased by the dilemma to move forward or back — was on display. Ishant repeatedly touched the 140-kph mark and the constant fear of getting that surprise in-coming ball was clearly on Ponting's mind.

Difficult period

To make things more difficult, Anil Kumble brought in Harbhajan Singh from the other end. Non-striker Simon Katich, aware of Ponting's abysmal India record, did his best to shield his skipper, and it was after he had bowled 14 deliveries that Harbhajan got the first crack at his long-time bunny. It was a perfect opening delivery from Ponting's point of view, flat and short, and the Australian dispatched it to the fence. But it was his second four — dancing down the track to meet the tossed-up ball and driving it through mid-off — that showed this wasn't the Ponting of old.

Rotation policy

The first-day track played true, but the ball didn't quite rush through after pitching. Ponting seemed to thrive in these conditions against the the spinners. There was enough time for him retract his steps if he wasn't quite to the pitch of the ball. Against both Harbhajan and Kumble, he would rock back and cut the ball after deciding against going on the front foot at the last minute. But the hallmark of the knock was the 45 singles he ran today — they not only helped keep the scoreboard ticking, but also denied Indian bowlers time to plan dismissals.

After comfortably dealing with his two main threats — Harbhajan and Ishant — early in his innings, the second half of the knock was a Ponting show that the Indian crowds hadn't seen in all these years but fans in all other countries had witnessed over the years.

Ishant's short balls outside off-stump were now dispatched with disdain to the cover boundary and when Zaheer Khan pitched it up, Ponting flicked him towards the square boundary. He saved his best for Harbhajan — slog-sweeping him over mid-wicket and lofting the ball with the turn.

At the end of the day, the scoreboard showed 'Ponting lbw Harbhajan' (a debatable decision since the ball may have been slipping down leg) but the figure at the end was different. After a series of 1s, 2s and 3s this time he had scored an overwhelming 123. After years of dominating on grass, Ponting finally had got a Grand Slam on clay.

Heading: Aussies did it one by one - Indian Express
Content:
Cricket Australia (CA) chief executive James Sutherland is delighted that Andrew Symonds has been working hard towards a comeback but made it clear that the all-rounder will have to earn his place in the side.

Symonds was sent home during the home series against Bangladesh after he skipped a compulsory team meeting to go fishing. He was then axed from the squad to tour India for a four-Test series. "I've had a couple of chats with him in the last couple of weeks. He understands that actions are the things that are really going to speak for him now and that's what he wants to concentrate on," Sutherland said about the apology by Symonds and the right noises he made to make amends.

"I've got a really good feeling about the way he is working towards coming back. There's nothing more that he wants right now than to be playing cricket for the Australian cricket team," he was quoted as saying by the Courier Mail.

The CA chief refused to set a date for Symonds's return. "I don't think there is any timeline. Andrew has quite rightly been careful not to build any expectations."

Heading: Ganguly lashes out in interview to Bengali daily - Indian Express
Content:
Two wickets in the final session changed the verdict from 'advantage Australia' to the much vaguer 'interestingly poised' at close of play on Thursday. With the visitors on 254/4 at the end of Day One, it means a prediction about where the match is headed will only be made during Friday's morning session.

While the Indians struggled for wickets, the Australian batsmen banked mainly on their running between wickets to keep the pressure off. On the eve of the match, when Ricky Ponting spoke about his team's new-age cricket, he had said how taking singles and rotating the strike were vital aspects. And it was clear that the 97 'ones' — almost 40 per cent of their total — played a big role for Australia during a hard day's grind.

Skipper Ricky Ponting, who ran 45 singles in his innings of 123, said later: "We achieved what we'd planned. We took a number of singles and, with the Indians pushing their fielders to the fence quite early in the game, it helped our cause. The singles helped us rotate the strike and that's why the Indian spinners didn't get too many overs at us for a long period of time."

Since the first-innings total on the pitch that is gradually expected to show wear and tear will be vital, the Aussies cut down on big, risky shots and settled for an uncharacteristic run-rate of 2.84. And with the left-right batting combinations swapping ends so frequently, bowlers found it difficult to maintain their length while constantly altering their line.

The plan was helped by the presence of old legs in the Indian inner ring. Rahul Dravid was in slips, the point-cover-gully cordon was manned by Sachin Tendulkar, VVS Laxman and Anil Kumble, while Sourav Ganguly shared duty at mid-on and mid-off with the the day's exhausted bowlers Zaheer, Ishant and Harbhajan. There were a couple of direct hits but no genuine run-out chance.

The second part of Ponting's so-called new-age gameplan is restricting the Indian batsmen from taking singles. "Putting pressure on the Indians when they are running between the wickets is crucial. If we can create a couple of run-outs in each Test innings, it'll be a huge achievement. We have a lot of good fieldsmen in the inner ring, guys like Michael Clarke," he said.

It remains to be seen if the Indians will manage to crack the code when it's their turn at the crease.

Heading: A cut above at 12-under - Indian Express
Content:
Sourav Ganguly has slammed the national selectors for the way he has been treated and said he decided to retire to save himself the humiliation of being treated as the "sacrificial lamb", according to an interview published in the Bengali daily Aaj Kaal. Ganguly was quoted as saying that there was no point in carrying on playing cricket if he was treated badly while some of the other players were spared.

"There is no point playing like this. I am not willing to play at their (selectors') mercy. They will pick you now and then dump you. Why should I be the sacrificial lamb all the time? It was difficult to accept," Ganguly, who announced his retirement from international cricket on Tuesday, was quoted as saying.

"If a gun is held at your head, how far can you bear it. That too after playing 450 matches. I played badly in only one series. But others are not dropped. I have scored the highest number of runs after comeback.

"How long would I have played? May be upto 2009. May be seven more Tests. For that I was not prepared to take any more humiliation," he added in the interview.

Ganguly reportedly told the paper that being dropped from the Irani Trophy Rest of India squad by the selection panel led by Vengsarkar was the last nail in the coffin and he thought he had faced enough humiliation by then.

"I never thought I will be out of the Irani team. I couldn't sleep for one month in anger, agony. Had this committee (new selection committee) come three years ago, things might have been different," the 36-year-old left hander was quoted as saying.

When reminded of Sunil Gavaskar's comments that he and VVS Laxman are always put under pressure, Ganguly reportedly said: "Anything can happen in Indian cricket. When Greg Chappell dropped me, he chose T P Singh to replace me. Where is he now?"

He added: "Some have not scored any runs in the last three series, some have not scored any runs during the last one year. Some have changed their hair style more number of times than the number of runs they have scored. I was dropped despite scoring the highest number of runs following my comeback."

Dropping from the Irani Cup hurt Ganguly so much that he considered it more painful than being sacked from the team after a spat with then coach Chappell.

Bad timing, says Sunny

Sunil Gavaskar said Ganguly's outburst against the selectors was "understandable" but he should have waited till the end of the Australia series. "I think the outburst is understandable, I only wish it had come after the series," Gavaskar said. "By saying all these things, he has not helped himself and I don't think he has helped harmony in the dressing room. He could have said all this after the series was over," Gavaskar told CNN-IBN.

Heading: Six shots back at DGC isn’t too bad - Indian Express
Content:
The almost-embarrassed nod to applause and a perpetual look of benign calmness might be familiar, but if one suspected a hidden showman in Liang Wen-chong, Thursday was the right day to be at the Delhi Golf Club.

The newly converted yoga practitioner, coming back after a swing-changing lay-off, playing his first competitive round at the intimidating DGC, and overshadowed in attention by the gallery trying to kick-start his playing partner Jyoti Randhawa's unresponsive game, Liang shot a course-record 12-under 60 in the opening round of the Indian Open.

As jaws dropped and confirmatory whispers swam around the sweaty afternoon, Asian Tour defending order of merit champion Liang, after an appreciable but comparatively conservative four-under at the turn, practically ran through his back nine. Eight birdies, with a solitary pause for breath on the fourth hole, meant that the 10-under that Shiv Kapur had set last year in a domestic tour event was ancient history. 12-under is also the best ever one-round score on the Asian Tour.

True to appearance, the self-analysis was understated. "It was quite intimidating to stand on the tees, looking at the narrow fairways, but everything fell into place today," China's Liang said.

International form

The second-best score was five shots back, Jeev Milkha Singh finally bringing his international form home. The seven-under 65 from Jeev came with five birdies and an eagle, drawn from a controlled approach to the greens and learning-manual bunker play.

Starting off on the 10th, right behind Liang and Randhawa, Jeev was busy giving a glimpse of his own dramatic self. Greeting fellow players, raking a bunker himself on one occasion, and clearly enjoying himself on way to his best ever round at this course.

His biggest putt was just about five feet, and the eagle came on the par-five first, holing in from the right greenside bunker.

Liang's blitz was clearly not infectious though, as Randhawa struggled throughout the day with his putter. There were three birdies, but just too many near-misses and five blundering bogeys gave the two-time defending champion a two-over 74, a score fourteen shots off the lead, and on a day of 51 under-par rounds, tied for the 92nd spot.

A bunch of three is tied for the third spot, Daniel Chopra sinking a 12-footer for eagle on the finishing 18th hole to join surprise name Sanjay Kumar and Lu Wen-teh at six-under 66.

Chopra was also bogey-less on the day, a birdie on his first hole followed by a period of stuttering with the speed of his putts. But he kept lining up the pars, and soon shed any possible nerves and the automatic programming of the fast PGA Tour greens to end the day with a broad smile.

"Today was my first competitive round with my new swing, and I'm starting to get comfortable," Chopra said. He was also clearly too pleased with his own best round at the DGC to worry too much about the six-shot deficit. "Six shots can be easily made up over three rounds of golf. I'm just happy with what I'm doing," Chopra said.

SSP Chowrasia was visibly bothered by his wrist, strapped, but clearly hurting every time he swung.

The normally dependable short game, too, gave up on him, as he finally carded a two-over 74. "I couldn't concentrate on anything because of the pain," Chowrasia said, choosing to leave the answer to the question on whether he's coming back on Friday open-ended.

Heading: ‘European Tour will withstand cash crisis’ - Indian Express
Content:
It was a great feeling today to try out all the techniques that I have been working on in the past few months.

I made some changes to my swing, and worked on a few other things with my coaches, and now they seem to be making a difference to my game. I just need to turn them into a habit.

What felt even better was the fact that I came back with a round of 66 — my best ever in a competition at the DGC. Playing there brought back all those feelings of nostalgia, as this is where I used to play as a kid.

I remember having come second at the Indian Open once in 1995, when Jim Rutledge won the title.

A year later, when the event was held in Calcutta, I was second again, tied with Jyoti Randhawa, when Japan's Hidezumi Shirakata won the title. In 2001 at the Classic Golf Resort, I didn't do so well.

Coming back to the DGC, I thought the course played well and easy. The bushes at the DGC are at their thickest, since we are playing at the end of the monsoon season. In winters, the bushes are thin and you at least can hope to have a shot. Here a small mistake means a big penalty.

The greens here take some getting used to. They are slower than what we play on in the US. So when you are standing on a putt, sometimes mentally you revert to what you are used to. It is my best-ever round at the DGC in tournament play. I have had a 63, but it was in a practice round long back. I am happy with my play today. I came back without a bogey, so it was great.

When I was at the early holes, I saw Jeev come back with his seven-under and Liang Wen-chong with a 12-under. I was one-under when I saw their scores. I remember Jeev's previous lowest of six-under 66 at the Hero Honda Masters.

More conservative

I held back and played more conservatively than I would normally do on any other course. I hit a 1-Iron and 2-iron. Actually both are 2-irons with similar shafts, it is just that I have changed the loft, so one is a strong 2-iron.

I was asked a lot about Liang Wen-chong. Sure, it is a great round, but no one is giving away the trophy yet. There are still three more rounds to go. I am six behind. Six shots at the DGC is really not too much.

As I mentioned earlier, I was consistent and it was my first real competitive round with the new swing. I suppose the more I trust it, it will become a habit for me.

Heading: Armstrong given UCI green signal - Indian Express
Content:
The European Tour's 'Race to Dubai' schedule for 2009 will be largely unaffected by the global financial crisis, the tour's director of international policy Keith Waters said on Thursday.

While the US PGA Tour's schedule for next year looks certain to be hit hard, the new-look 'Race to Dubai' schedule, with tournaments offering around 140 million euro in prize money, could have been saved by negotiations carried out over a year ago.

"The two real major pillars in terms of confirming financial support for the 2009 season, television rights and a huge input from Dubai, were all worked out about 12 or 14 months ago," said Waters.

"I think we are confident that our schedule will go ahead as planned. There are no assurances, of course, because we are in the throes of something that is pretty well unprecedented. We have also worked pretty hard in the last two or three weeks to make sure everything will go ahead. Where the European Tour gains over its counterpart over the Atlantic, where several tournaments sponsored by banks and motor companies are threatened, is in its spread of sponsors," Waters said.

"We do have a different model to the PGA. We have more diverse sources of income than in America. And I think that diversity will make a difference."

Heading: Even as options dwindle, Alonso stays firm about move - Indian Express
Content:
Cycling's governing body is relaxing its own rules to allow Lance Armstrong to make his road race comeback in Australia in January next year.

The International Cycling Union said the seven-time Tour de France champion can compete in the January 20-25 Tour Down Under, his first race since coming out of retirement after three years. A strict application of dope testing rules would not have allowed the 37-year-old American to compete until February 1, 2009, six months after he filed paperwork with the US Anti-Doping Agency.

But the UCI said on Wednesday that Armstrong could return early because its drug-testing standards have improved since the rule was drawn up four years ago. "Riders are now subject to a much-reinforced system of monitoring compared to that of the past," the governing body said in a statement. "Lance Armstrong has and will be the subject of very strict monitoring throughout the period running up to his return to the peloton."

Answer to critics

Armstrong's comeback is meant to draw attention to his global campaign to fight cancer, a disease he survived before winning seven straight Tours from 1999-2005. It is also a defiant stand against critics who doubt he could have achieved those victories without the use of performance-enhancing drugs.

Now he is liable to be tested at any time without notice and will have his own biological passport as part of a UCI-backed scheme to monitor possible doping offenses. Riders must give a series of blood and urine samples which allow a World Anti-Doping Agency-accredited laboratory to measure abnormal fluctuations in body readings.

Armstrong said last month he was tested in late August, and has enlisted a personal anti-doping expert in Don Catlin, who will make his test results available to the public. Catlin, who ran the first anti-doping lab in the United States at UCLA for 25 years, will freeze and keep samples of Armstrong's blood to be analysed in the future.

Armstrong will not be paid for returning to the saddle and the testing costs will be covered by his Kazakhstan-based team Astana. Armstrong has suggested he might enter the Paris-Nice classic stage race in March, and compete in South Africa before taking part in the Giro d'Italia in May. He will attempt to win the Tour de France an eighth time in July.

Heading: Delays push cost of government infrastructure projects up 13.4% - Indian Express
Content:
Fernando Alonso refused on Thursday to rule out a move from Renault despite being left with few alternatives for 2009. The double world champion had been linked with a move to BMW-Sauber until they decided this week to stick with Poland's Robert Kubica and Germany's Nick Heidfeld. The removal of that option left Alonso with a likely toss-up between Honda, who have made their interest clear and are waiting on the Spaniard's decision, and a further season at Renault. Toro Rosso are the only other team with a clear vacancy.

"I have a contract with Renault for next year and the possibility to take that extension or not," Alonso told reporters at the Japanese Grand Prix. "I'm not waiting (in order) to make your lives impossible. I prefer to wait until the end of the season. After Brazil I will make my decision."

Alonso said his surprise win in Singapore last month, his first victory in more than a year and Renault's first since the Spaniard won his second title with them in 2006, would have no bearing. "It's the same question as always," he smiled.

"On the Saturday we had the fuel pump problems and I was out of Q2 (the second stage of qualifying) and the question was would it change my decision. The day after I won the race and it was 'Will this change your decision?' Nothing changed my decision. It will be more important than one single result. It's more about understanding next year's regulations, next year's car, the aerodynamics, whatever. We need to pay attention to that."

Alonso added: "We were extremely lucky with the race — safety cars, tyre decisions, everything was perfect for us. In a normal race, Ferrari and McLaren are still unbeatable."

With the door to his first choice Ferrari closing on him last month when the champions extended Kimi Raikkonen's contract, Alonso said he was not surprised to hear BMW-Sauber announce an unchanged line-up. "It was never a possibility," shrugged the 27-year-old. (Reuters)

'Removing Canadian GP wrong move'

Formula One may be damaged by the decision to axe the Canadian Grand Prix from next year's calendar, BMW-Sauber boss Mario Theissen said on Thursday. The governing International Automobile Federation (FIA) this week issued a revised calendar, drawn up by the sport's commercial supremo Bernie Ecclestone, with no slot for the Montreal race.

"It's the opposite of what we want to see," Theissen told reporters. "The North American market still is the biggest one, not just for BMW. It's always been difficult to set foot into the US but Canada especially." Theissen complained that dropping Canada made little financial sense at a time when the sport is looking at ways to cut costs to ensure its survival.

Heading: US may take part ownership in banks - Indian Express
Content:
The exchequer might have a tough time accounting for this. The cumulative cost of all 519 central government-funded infrastructure projects of over Rs 100 crore is expected to rise by another Rs 46,000 crore by the time they are completed. Bulk of the escalation is in Railway projects.

According to the Flash Report on Central Sector Projects for April 2008, prepared by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, Railways projects saw one of the biggest percentage spikes in their anticipated costs. For a total of 138 projects, the cost is expected to almost double from Rs 37,863 crore to Rs 70,237 crore by the time they are completed. At present, the revised cost estimate stands at Rs 41,741 crore, 10.4 per cent higher than the original cost.

The report notes that the total cost of all infrastructure projects under implementation is expected to go up 13.4 per cent from Rs 3,44,119 crore to Rs 3,90,230 crore. The biggest reason for the cost overrun is the delays in their execution.

Overall, 258 projects are running behind schedule, 13 are ahead of schedule and 146 others are running on time. Of the 53 projects that reported additional delays of up to 16 months in April this year, 50 are concentrated in just four sectors — power, railways, road transport and highways and telecommunications. Steel and petroleum, on the other hand, reported delays in one and two projects, respectively of 1-12 months.

In roads and highways, a total of 25 projects reported delays over the previous month's expectation of up to 12 months. The report cited problems such as tardy progress by the contractor, termination of contracts, law and order situation in the region, late award of contract, etc. as the primary reasons for the delays. However, it added that the project authorities had failed to provide any specific reasons for the delays.

In railways and telecom, too, 10 and nine projects respectively saw additional delays of up to 12-14 months, but project authorities failed to provide any justification for them. Six projects in the power sector saw further delays of up to 16 months for various reasons such as non-resolution of funding issues, delay of supply in material, labour problems, delay in award of contract, etc.
