There are also future stars like Yuki Bhambri in tennis, and the next generation of shooters and boxers.

The Army Sports Institute, after a listless 2008 Olympics, will test out their new batch of pugilists — with the Beijing medal-inspiration, as fresh-minted as the coats of turpentine paint, making its way onto buildings and even mountains. Yes, one hillock is actually being splashed with paint here, as part of finishing touches to the event.

Opinion stands divided over the preparedness of the venues. Competition-ready on most accounts, the external beautification remains, though a general sense of chaos prevails owing to security. Sandwiched between the song and dance of the opening and closing ceremonies — essential frivolities — are five days of competition, and a chance for the city's residents to choose India's sporting heroes of the coming decade, test their prowess, separate the wheat from the chaff; seeing it all for themselves. Pune is well-suited for the job too — a natural launchpad for athletes looking for a take-off, even as Raju goes trendy and becomes Jigrr.

Heading: Mutatkar reaches semi-finals - Indian Express
Content:
"I have to do this work myself, otherwise it will not be done right," stated a visibly tired coach of the Indian athletics team Suresh Babu, crouched at a table in front of a computer getting his team members accredited on Friday night.

With just a day to go for the Commonwealth Youth Games to commence, instead of working out with his wards on the track, the former Olympian, who dominated the jump events on the national scene during the seventies, was engaged in filling up forms and checking the spelling of the names of his boys and girls. "We had gone to the stadium at 2 O'clock today to collect the kits, but that too did not take place," informed Babu who was engaged in the clerical activity all evening. "I have done 28 names and the rest of the 45 will have to be done tomorrow," said the coach as the night wore on.

It was quite an organisational chaos with no one seeming to be in charge at the accreditation office and frequent computer glitches, along with over-worked volunteers throwing up their hands in sheer desperation.

Heading: Now or never for Bagan - Indian Express
Content:
Leading 20-17 in her decider in Bulgaria, Aditi Mutatkar's mind threatened to drag her back to her last Grand Prix final in Germany where she squandered match points. But the Pune shuttler, playing the quarters at this GP meet, killed a few demons when she beat Indonesian Maria Elfira Christina of Indonesia 14-21, 21-14, 21-18 to make the semi-finals.

Playing defensively in the first game against the higher-ranked and fourth-seeded rival, Mutatkar, seeded fifth, changed the pace of her game in the second. The third game went level till the Indian, who should break into the Top 50 now, jumped to a 20-17 lead — a familiar position, from her last week at Germany's Bitburger. "I went more aggressive at that point, and that did it. I was relieved. I just wanted to win, I know how bad you feel when you don't win close matches. I thought I'd had enough," said Mutatkar after her 1 hour 10 minute-long match. She next plays local hope and top-20 Petya Nedelcheva. "Playing the Asians, we tend to tire out. Today I'm glad I could outlast her," she said.

Heading: Slight improvement, but work to be done - Indian Express
Content:
It's now or never for Mohun Bagan. If the green-and-maroons want to keep their title hopes alive, they have to win against Sporting Clube de Goa in their third round I-League match at Margao on Saturday.

Sporting are on a high after two successive wins over Vasco Sports Club and Mohammedan Sporting, while Bagan, on the other hand, have only one point after two home matches. Though there is still a lot of football to be played this season, a title will seem an unlikely possibility for the Kolkata giants should they falter in this outing.

Injury is a huge cause of concern for Bagan, with Baichung Bhutia among the absentees. Coach Karim Bencherifa, however, put up a brave face. "We had a decent start as our team performed well, but were unlucky as we missed good scoring chances. We have worked on our mistakes and hopefully the team will perform to its potential," he said.

Dipak Mondal and Habibur Rahman will return to strengthen the defence, but without a playmaker, building up an attack is difficult. The onus is on Lalkamal Bhowmick to fill the vacuum.

Sporting's midfield has gelled very well, with Harmanjot Khabra, Micky Fernandes, Wilton Gomes and Joseph Pereira combining like a well-oiled machine. Pereira's partnership with Gomes on the left has resulted in teasing crosses that keep the rival defence guessing. Up front, there is Junior Obagbemiro, who has already scored three goals. Another Nigerian, Natalin is likely to make his debut on Saturday.

Sporting's defence is yet to concede a goal in this tournament. Naturally, their coach Vishwas Goaunkar is confident of maintaining the winning streak.

"After our impressive performance against Mohammedan Sporting, we are on a high. We want to keep the momentum going. The boys have the potential to perform even better. Natalin will provide more sharpness to our attack," he said.

Heading: Liang still five shots clear - Indian Express
Content:
Sometimes what we do on the golf course does not get reflected in the scorecard. That's what happened this afternoon. I think I played far better than the two-under 70 my card shows, but I will take eight-under at the halfway stage.

The good thing is that despite a 70, I made up one. I was six behind after the first day and now I am five behind. A slight improvement, but still some work to be done.

Liang, though, has been on fire. He seemed to be running away after a four-under front nine, but then the DGC had its say. He ended with a 71, with four bogeys in seven holes.

From an Indian viewpoint, there are quite a few home players in the fray, even though Jeev Milkha had a disappointing finish. Ashok Kumar, Sanjay Kumar and Harinder Gupta are in the top-10, just a shot behind me. Jyoti Randhawa also ensured weekend action with a 69.

I had a flawless front nine and was four under — things looked good.

Then I had one bad tee shot on the eighth, which was the second last hole for me, and I had to pay a heavy price. In fact, even the shot was not bad, I just got a bad bounce and it landed in an unplayable situation; I ended up with a double bogey. That was a little disappointing after a flawless front nine.

But I am feeling good about my game. The changes that I have been working on in the last few months are coming on nicely. Soon things should all fall in place.

I wanted to move to a new level and that's why I went for these changes. I knew it would take time and I am still in the process, though it's coming close to becoming a habit.

The course is playing great. The fairways have been the best I have seen at the DGC. The golf course looks spectacular.

The scores have been great, too. I never thought I would be here to play in a tournament where someone scores a 60 on the first day. Then I see an 11-under on the second day from a Dutch pro, Guido Van Der Valik.

It's awesome to have two people play the course in 60 and 61 on two successive days.

As for my plans for the next two days, I want to just keep going, play steady and make a few birdies. However, I expect the pins to be tougher over the weekend.

Heading: Make borders irrelevant, PM tells Valley, regrets deaths and curfew - Indian Express
Content:
Dutch Guido van der Valk, pudgy-faced, wide-eyed, European Tour second-stringer, was to come to Delhi for the Indian Open in 2007, but his visa didn't land on time. The delay this time was of a different kind, and of just one day, but it still mattered. Van der Valk shot an eye-popping 11-under in his second round at the Delhi Golf Club on Friday. A day before, the 61 would've been a new course record, and a match of the Asian Tour best score. Coming a day after Liang Wen-chong's 12-under, it raised a few eyebrows and the 28-year-old from the obscurity of tied 126th to the scrutiny of tied sixth on the leaderboard.

Despite an oscillating one-under 71, Liang still leads by five shots over Daniel Chopra, who soured his four-birdie round with a trip to the DGC jungle on his second-last hole, the par-five eighth, giving him a double bogey. Overnight second, Jeev Milkha Singh lost his putting touch and his way, as four bogeys on the back nine dropped him down to two-over 74 for the round and in tied 17th spot.

Jyoti Randhawa's game looked edgy, but worked enough to get the defending champion into the weekend. He shot three-under 69 to be one-under for the tournament, two inside the cut mark of one-over. Randhawa was level par for the tournament as he stared at a four-foot par putt on the 16th when he realised just how important that could turn out to be. He dropped that in, hit a bulls-eye shot off the tee to be three feet away on the next, the par-three 17th, and birdied that to be comfortably over. He's 12 shots off the lead. SSP Chowrasia shot an even par but missed the cut.

Liang had obviously recreated the morning schedule from Thursday, and the results seemed headed the same way. With not two wrong shots in succession, birdies kept rolling in as he went from 12-under to 16-under, running away from everyone. The turnaround, though, came right at the turn. He was just off the green with his second shot on the par-four, but the five-foot putt for par stayed out as Liang finally blinked. With his big lead, the bogey was more technical glitch than anything, but it broke the spell. Liang's picture-perfect swinging from Thursday was gone, and with it the concentration. Putts stopped just short as he bogeyed five holes on the back nine, three coming in succession from the 13th to the 15th. "After that bogey I wanted to bounce back quickly and lost my concentration," Liang said "I have to keep it steady."

Ashok Kumar's seven birdies on Thursday had been wasted in two double bogeys and a bogey. He kept up the drama in his second round, but changed the theme. Six birdies and one bogey gave him a five-under round as he moved into the top-three spot.

Van der Valk, with an ordinary five-over 77 in his first proper round at the DGC on Thursday, decided there was no harm in getting a little more aggressive to try make it on the richer side of the cut mark. So out came the driver and some pluck and the lost pieces of what seemed like an unsolvable puzzle on the first day all fell into place. "I was telling myself to try and shoot a five-under to make the cut," van der Valk said. "So it came as a big, pleasant surprise." Starting on the 10th, van der Valk's hitting was so accurate that the five birdies on his front nine all came with putts less than 10 feet long. There were four more birdies and an eagle on the par-five first. Giving the Asian Tour qualifying school a try after coming to the continent for a world cup qualifier and liking the atmosphere, van der Valk fell in love with the people. "It's like the friends' tour or something," he said. It was time to make friends with its golf courses on Friday.

Heading: Soon, you won’t be able to cross 100 km/h on expressways - Indian Express
Content:
Fresh from his biggest policy triumph, the Indo-US nuclear deal, Prime Minister Manmohan Singh did not announce any new policy initiative on Kashmir on Friday but said the Centre wanted borders to be irrelevant so that there was no difference between Srinagar and Muzaffarabad.

The Prime Minister, in a press conference called after an all-party meeting, outlined an already laid-out framework to address the problems of the state and regretted the recent loss of lives in Kashmir. He repeated his condolences to the bereaved families several times during his briefing while two people were killed and 75 injured in protests against his visit on Friday.

"There is a tinge of sadness this time because of the recent incidents of violence which have caused concern to all of us," PM Singh said. "I express my condolences to the relatives of those who have lost their lives in the violence." In fact, Singh also regretted the imposition of curfew but said "it was necessary to do so to prevent violence and loss of life and property."

His emphasis was on the recent thaw in bilateral relations with Pakistan, suggesting it will help resolve Kashmir as well. "While we cannot change borders, we can make them irrelevant. We want to reach a level in our bilateral relationship whereby a Kashmiri experiences no difference between Srinagar and Muzaffarabad and old ways of thinking become irrelevant".

Singh said that there were winds of change in the subcontinent. He said in his recent meeting with President Zardari, he had invited him to work with India "to usher in a new era of subcontinental cooperation". "Economics, technology and travel are altering older mindsets of suspicion, fear and hostility," Singh said.

He said that it was undeniable that much has changed between India and Pakistan in the past few years. "Trade, people-to-people contact, cultural exchanges and, most of all, the desire to move on are altering the landscape of our relationship." Singh emphasised that a "strong, stable and prosperous Pakistan is in India's interest."

As for his overtures to separatists, Singh had little to offer them except for an "open-ended invitation" to all sections of the public opinion. "The Government will welcome dialogue with all sections of people. This also includes those who have so far opted to stay out of the political process," Singh said.

His accent, however, was more on the development of the state. Singh said that his government sought normalcy in the state so that tasks of development could be accelerated. He talked about the investments in roads, railways and airline connectivity. He also announced that J&K would get one Indian Institute of Management and a Central university in the 11th plan, besides upgradation of Srinagar and Jammu medical colleges to the level of All India Institute of Medical Sciences.

When asked about the recent terror incidents across the country and their security fallout, Singh said that his government will act tough with the terrorists. "But we should avoid profiling of the communities in our war on terror," he said.

Heading: Week after Nano pullout, CPM blames Tata too for fiasco - Indian Express
Content:
Get ready to speed - legally. The Ministry of Road Transport & Highways is set to notify later this month higher speed limits for all categories of vehicles, raising speed ceilings that were fixed 17 years ago.

Cars will be able to drive at 100 km/h on expressways, 80 km/h on 4-6 lane national highways, 60 km/h on 2-lane highways and 50 km/h on major district roads and urban arterials. (See chart)

The speeds are part of the recommendations of a five-member committee set up by the ministry last year to frame new limits consistent with India's improved road infrastructure and upgraded automobile technology.

Most countries allow speeds up to 120 km/h or expressways. Austria and UAE allow speeds up to 160km/h on some stretches.

"The plan was to make speed limits more realistic. We decided after consultations with traffic experts. The current speed limit is low, and hence you have vehicles overspeeding," said a committee member.

Heading: All hands on board: PM’s economic team calls off  trips to U S - Indian Express
Content:
It's not just Mamata Banerjee. A week after Ratan Tata decided to pull the Nano project out of West Bengal, the CPM has apportioned a share of the blame to the industrialist as well for taking an "unreasonable position".

In an article in the party mouthpiece, People's Democracy, CPM Politburo member Sitaram Yechury said the Tatas' stand that they would not remain in Singur unless they got everyone's cooperation was "unreasonable". He said the administration had discharged its responsibilities in maintaining law and order.

"The Tatas, however, took a stand that unless everybody cooperates, they are not going to continue to remain in Singur. One can, surely, disagree with such a position. For, after all, no one can say that they shall build their house in a locality only when all others living there will give an assurance that their house will not be burgled. However, like Mamata Banerjee, the Tatas also have an equal right to take an unreasonable position," he has said.

Heading: Despite rate-cut pill, global flu batters Sensex - Indian Express
Content:
Key members of Prime Minister Manmohan Singh's economic team, P Chidambaram, Montek Singh Ahluwalia and Kamal Nath, have called off scheduled official trips to the U S to tackle the ripple effects of the global financial turmoil at home.

Finance minister Chidambaram cancelled his visit to the IMF-World Bank informal meetings during the weekend ahead of the plenary session on Monday. He was also slated to take part in a meeting of the G-20 finance ministers, to be chaired by U S Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson.

In fact, New Delhi and Washington have decided to put off the annual meeting of the Indo-US CEOs forum in New York next Tuesday.

Government sources said the decision was taken by Prime Minister Manmohan Singh on Thursday. Both Commerce and Industry Minister Kamal Nath and Planning Commission Deputy Chairman Ahluwalia, key members of the bilateral strategic economic group, cancelled their plans to be available back home to enable quicker decision-making.

Reserve Bank of India Governor Duvvuri Subbarao and economic affairs secretary Ashok Chawla are already in Washington for the Fund-Bank meetings that officially begin on October 13. Sources said Subbarao too has been asked to be prepared to return on short notice, if required.

Both sides decided to postpone the Indo-U S CEOs forum since Paulson, US Commerce Secretary Carlos Gutierrez and Trade Representative Susan Schwab — all members of the bilateral group—¿ are busy aiding President George W. Bush in the firefight.

Besides, William Harrison, former chairman of JP Morgan Chase, Vikram Pandit of Citigroup, co-chair and a member of the CEOs forum from the US side, are also battling their own troubles. In India too, Ratan Tata, co-chair of the bilateral group, is perturbed by the magnitude of the crisis that has spread like a contagion from the US to Europe and the Asia-Pacific.

Heading: Shouldering Trouble - Indian Express
Content:
India's benchmark Sensex was today dragged into the global stampede of selling as the financial turmoil that started in the US spread like a contagion and killed market sentiment across the world. Global stock markets plunged by up to 10 per cent on Friday amidst mounting fears that this week's efforts by central banks and governments to stabilise the credit markets have failed.

Almost immediately after the markets opened, the Sensex plunged by over 1,000 points. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervened to ease liquidity in the system by cutting the cash reserve ratio (the portion of deposits banks have to keep with the central bank) by another one per cent, thus taking the total reduction this week to 1.5 per cent, and releasing Rs 60,000 crore (over $ 12 billion) into the funds-starved system. In the backdrop of tight liquidity, the finance ministry cancelled a Rs 10,000 crore government borrowing plan.

Finance Minister P Chidambaram constituted a group comprising top bankers headed by Finance Secretary Arun Ramnathan to advise the government on liquidity requirements within a week. He also assured cash-strapped markets that the government would inject more funds into the system in the next 10-12 days through the supplementary demands for grants, which will come up for approval before Parliament later this month.

Ruling out any systemic problem, Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) chairman C B Bhave said there was no unusual activity in the stock market, and no short selling by institutions in the cash market. Assuring more steps if needed, the RBI said, "market participants are assured that the Reserve Bank stands ready to respond swiftly to meet any liquidity requirements that may arise in the context of the highly volatile external situation."

The new RBI measures and assurances by the government did not have much impact on the market, though. The BSE Sensex ended down 800.51 points or 7.07% to 10,527.86. The index lost 16 per cent during the week, its worst performance since 1990. It is now 10,678.91 points or 50.35% below its all-time high of 21,206.77, struck on January 10, 2008.

ICICI Bank plunged as much as 28 per cent to its lowest in almost four years, before trimming losses to 19 per cent after the bank's joint managing director Chanda Kochhar said the bank has sufficient liquidity and it has never used rupee funds for its international growth initiatives.

Cutting the CRR to the 7.50 per cent level, the RBI said, "In the context of the abrupt changes in the international financial environment, it is important to note that the macroeconomic fundamentals of the Indian economy are strong and resilient and that India's financial system is sound, well-capitalised and well-regulated." Since Monday's 50-basis point CRR cut, the global situation has worsened further. "International stock markets and money markets had been adversely affected in a significant manner," the RBI said.

Bank bailouts, liquidity injections and interest rate cuts across the world failed to quell global investor anxiety. Asian and European stocks tumbled — Thailand fell 9.6 per cent, Singapore 7.3 per cent, Philippines 8.3 per cent and Hong Kong 7.2 per cent. Japan's Nikkei share average tumbled 9.6 per cent, its biggest rout since 1987. Trading was stopped in Austria, Russia, Iceland, Romania, Indonesia and Ukraine, while Milan suspended share dealings in nearly half of its stocks because of excessive losses. The latest woes in Europe came after the Dow Jones index in the US closed 679 points, or 7.3 per cent lower, at 8,579.19 on Thursday, its first close below 9,000 in five years.

Meanwhile, the RBI has said it "would respond swiftly and even preemptively to any adverse external developments impinging on domestic financial stability, price stability and inflation expectations and the continuation of the growth momentum of the Indian economy."

Experts don't rule out a cut in policy rates (like bank rate, repo and reverse repo rates). "Given the worsening global situation, cuts are not ruled out. However, with growth in M3 (money supply) at 21%, credit at 26% and inflation at 12%, the RBI has little leeway unless a sharp fall in commodity prices results in quicker easing in inflation to single digit levels," said Rohini Malkani, Economist, Citigroup India.

Heading: Recognise the power of good nutrition - Indian Express
Content:
I could blame the weightlifting, the bench presses and overhead military lifts that put the shoulder under pressure. I could blame the arm-twisting I get three times a week from my aikido buddies.

Instead I have decided to blame Douglas Engelbart, the man who, perhaps unwittingly, has put a generation of rotator cuffs, shoulders and other body parts at risk. In the 1960s, Engelbart invented the computer mouse, an ingenious device that evolved into a cheap, mass-produced and pretty much unavoidable tool of modern office life. It is, I feel, a likely culprit for the nagging pain that has developed in my right shoulder in the past year or so.

Of course, maybe all the other stuff has had an aggravating role. But when I think about how I have used my right and left arms over the years, the mouse is the most prominent difference between them.

I am by nature left-handed and have spent a lifetime throwing balls, swinging tennis rackets and otherwise favouring my left side when it comes to activity. But I "mouse" with the right hand — too often with the arm extended and the shoulder twisted in exactly the wrong ways.

Undertrained. Weaker. Overstressed. The right side had all the ingredients for trouble. I am now convinced that hours manipulating the mouse wore down the cartilage in a couple of my shoulder bones, strained some of the small connective muscles in the area and led to the diagnosis I got recently from Jonas Rudzki at Washington Orthopaedics and Sports Medicine: arthritis in the acromioclavicular joint and rotator cuff tendinitis.

I turned down the cortisone. The physical therapy is under way.

If you want a surefire way to start a conversation with anyone older than 40, talk about shoulders. Maybe half will have had a problem, and of those who haven't, many can expect to as they age. The symptoms can range from an annoying twinge to a deep throb that interferes with sleep to a loss of motion.

In my case, wear and tear on the AC joint, where the part of the shoulder blade called the acromion meets the clavicle, has worn away the cushion of cartilage between the two bones, the condition known as osteoarthritis. More problematic (at least in my case) is the rotator cuff: a set of four small muscles that help hold the arm in the shoulder socket and stabilise it as it moves.

Why is the shoulder so vulnerable?

It is perhaps the most complicated joint in the body, responsible for the movement of a limb that is designed to go through a wide range of motion in several planes. (To get a sense of the shoulder's diversity, try tracing the same lines in the air with your knee or foot that you can with your hand.)

What's more, it does this while fighting gravity. The hip, for example, also has wide range. But in its case the top of the leg nestles deeply into the socket, and the weight of the body on top of it helps stabilise the whole mechanism. The shoulder, by contrast, has a comparatively shallow socket with connective tissue that is hanging onto a limb that, even at rest, is constantly being tugged on.

Modern life hasn't helped. Even with a desk, computer and chair arrangement that complies with Occupational Safety and Health Administration recommendations, how many of us still hunch over our keyboards? That position prevents the muscles of the upper and middle back from doing their jobs — part of which is to support the scapula (the shoulder blade) and synchronise it with the motion of the arm. If you use your arms and hands while in this position, the rotator cuff muscles end up under duress.

Multiply stress and bad habits over a couple of decades, add poor posture and a decline in blood flow associated with ageing, and the shoulder becomes a breeding ground for aches and pains.

Fortunately, rotator cuff injuries do not typically involve the type of full tears that baseball pitchers or other athletes suffer (or that might occur in a severe weight room trauma), and therefore don't require surgery. Instead, they can be treated with an assortment of rehabilitation strategies.

In my second session with physical therapist Patrick Kennelly, he was able to massage and loosen the muscle beneath the shoulder blade, and it made an immediate difference once that part of the body could move more freely.

He also recommended shoulder and upper-back exercises, some of which seemed to be taken straight from the yoga playbook; a sequence done with the knees and one hand on the ground, for example, that involved extending the arm in front of the head, threading it under the body and then lifting it to the sky.

"Yoga is our enemy," Kennelly said jokingly. "It keeps people out of here." Yoga teachers, in fact, frequently note that joints do not have a dedicated blood supply and are nourished when motion causes the secretion of synovial fluid — hence all the twisting and contortions of a standard yoga session.

The concept is important, but local medical experts say it is often lost on people who are having trouble. The intuitive response is more like "if it hurts, leave it alone". In fact, in the case of joint problems and arthritis, motion and activity are critical.

"Biomechanically it can only get worse," said Jay Greenstein, head of the local Sport and Spine Rehab clinics. "If you feel the pain and don't do the activity, you are losing out. It is going to catch up with you. It won't be [while you are] lifting weights at the gym; it will be getting something out of the cupboard."

The recommended exercises are, however, painstaking and tedious — not ones that will leave you spent and feeling as if you have pushed your body to its limits. Quite the contrary, they involve light weights and potentially dozens of repetitions. The rotator cuff is not meant to bear heavy loads but is "always active" and needs to be trained for endurance, said T Moorman, the head of sports medicine at Duke University Medical School.

The sequence that Kennelly provided me involved using resistance bands to strengthen the cuff and stretches to loosen the upper back. More rotation in the back means more help supporting the shoulder and arm when you reach out or across the body.

In my case, this is all to fix a problem. The same types of exercises can (should!) be done by anyone who is healthy to make sure their cuff stays strong and injury-free. Upper-back exercises, yoga — there is much else that can help.

And, just like your mother told you, stand up straight.

Heading: Discussing death is good for patients: study - Indian Express
Content:
If I were to search for a flipside in my otherwise highly fulfilling vocation as a nutritional consultant it would have to be the persistent — and at times annoying — habit of many patients who come to me seeking magic-bullet dietary remedies for treating ailments or for weight reduction.

This happens even after I have explained patiently that it is far easier to gain weight than to lose it. This dictum of mine on weight management has a natural corollary that says any nutritional intervention for treating afflictions will generally take time to bear fruit. The plus side of these nutritional remedies is that they tend to have lasting benefits with almost no side effects. I sometimes despair that most of us fail to appreciate or recognise the power of good nutrition. This does put our science and its practice at a disadvantage when compared with the high-profile surgical or antibiotic-based interventions for treating health disorders. The other disadvantage of not paying enough attention and respect to healthy nutrition is that inappropriate nutrition can cause grave and long-term harm. This message is particularly relevant for women who are expecting or are planning to have babies.

A very significant and credible study published a decade ago revealed that the nutrition available to a baby in the womb affects the health of the individual even in adulthood. Low-birth weight babies are generally predisposed to many problems later on in life, such as high blood pressure, glucose intolerance and heart diseases. The persistence of the effects of poor nutrition into adulthood is almost uncanny. However, before mothers begin to panic, let me say they need not worry. Nutrition-based interventions can help combat possible harm caused by low birth weight. It has been noted by several studies that physical exercise and appropriate diet does negate the harm done in the womb or even just after birth to a great extent.

Hence, for all mothers-to-be, I want this to be a message in loud and clear terms — the best investment for your child is to eat right when expecting. If you live your present well the future of your child will be well taken care of.

Heading: Your Age on Your Page - Indian Express
Content:
Talking about death may be upsetting but a doctor's frank discussion with a terminally ill person does no harm and provides numerous benefits to patients and those close to them, US researchers said.

Patients who had talks about what type of care they want — and do not want — as they near death experienced a better quality of life in their waning days than those who did not, and they were no more apt to experience depression, worry or sadness, the study found.

The patients received fewer aggressive medical interventions, such as being placed on a ventilator to breathe, being resuscitated or being sent to an intensive care unit, the researchers reported in the Journal of the American Medical Association. And the patients sought hospice care earlier. In addition, their informal caregiver, usually a spouse or adult child, was less likely to experience major depression in the months after the patient's death if aggressive medical interventions were avoided.

"The major findings are that end-of-life discussions have cascading benefits for patients and their loved ones," said Dr Alexi Wright of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston, one of the researchers.

Wright's team said previous studies indicated that doctors and patients are ambivalent about talking death and frequently avoid the discussions.

A doctor or a patient can initiate a discussion, which gives people the chance to define their goals and expectations for medical care as they approach death, Wright said.

"Talking about death is difficult. And the reason we started the study was we wanted to see if the conversations were worth it," Wright said. "We expected to find more evidence of psychological harm associated with the conversations but didn't find any."

The study involved 332 terminally ill cancer patients in Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Texas, of whom 123 reported having had such a conversation with their doctor. These patients were more likely to accept that their cancer would kill them and expressed desire for comfort care near death over life-extending therapies, the researchers found.

On average, the patients were followed for the final 4-1/2 months of life. The researchers then assessed the emotional health of the caregiver an average of 6-1/2 months later.

Wright said the way a patient died influenced the way their loved ones lived on. People whose loved ones died in an intensive care unit (ICU) were three times more likely to have major depression than those whose loved ones did not die in an ICU.

Heading: Nicotine gum benefits pregnant smokers - Indian Express
Content:
ZERO TO 20

Microwaves pose burn injury risk to children

Microwave ovens pose a serious safety hazard to young children, a new study of scald burn injuries published in the Pediatrics indicates. Hot foods or liquids from microwave ovens were the fourth leading cause of scald injuries in children under 5 years old, a review of records from the University of Chicago Burn Center shows. It can be difficult to keep young children away from kitchen hazards, especially if an adult is alone at home and trying to cook dinner. Parents should keep a child well away from the stove if the child must be in the kitchen while food preparation is under way. For example, by seating younger children on a high chair or setting up a safe play area.

20 TO 50

Eating dark chocolate may keep heart healthy

Eating dark chocolate regularly may help lower levels of inflammation, which is strongly associated with heart and blood vessel disease, states Italian researchers in the Journal of Nutrition. The presence of inflammation was determined by measuring levels C-reactive protein (CRP), a biomarker for coronary artery disease. The range of CRP levels seen in the dark chocolate consuming group corresponds to a "mild" risk of cardiovascular disease, while CRP levels in the non-consumers would be associated with "moderate" risk. The benefits were seen when people ate up to one 20-gram serving of dark chocolate every 3 days, but eating more chocolate wasn't more beneficial; in fact, effects on CRP levels "tended to disappear" at higher consumption levels.

50 AND ABOVE

Obesity tied to early heart attack

Heart attacks occur earlier in people who are overweight or obese, compared to normal-weight people, states a new research published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology. The average age at first heart attack was 74.6 years in the leanest patients and 58.7 years in the most obese. Women were predominant in both the groups, the investigators found. The researchers determined that compared to study subjects with a normal body mass index — BMI between 18.6 and 25.0 — subjects who were overweight — BMI between 25.1 and 30.0 — had a first heart attack some 3.5 years earlier. Obese individuals — BMI between 30.1 and 35.0 — had a first heart attack 6.8 years earlier than normal-weight subjects and for severely obese individuals — BMI greater than 40 — it was 12.0 years.

Heading: Stopping a woman from access to husband’s house, personal goods is economic abuse: court - Indian Express
Content:
Prosecutors in an Italian court Thursday asked the key middleman in the IAF's VVIP chopper deal whether the initials 'AP' in an alleged "budget sheet" for bribes to politicians referred to Ahmed Patel, the political secretary of UPA chairperson Sonia Gandhi.

The middleman, Guido Haschke, who has consistently denied bribing Indian officials or politicians, replied that he did not know who or what 'AP' stood for.

As first reported by The Indian Express, Italian prosecutors had last month produced a handwritten document they alleged was a "budget" drawn up by two middlemen — Haschke and Christian Michel — which purportedly lists initials of Indian politicians and designations of bureaucrats and IAF officers who allegedly had to be "handled" to fix the Rs 3,546 crore deal.

The alleged "budget sheet" detailed how kickbacks of 51 million euros would be divided and under the heading "POL" — Haschke has claimed this referred to Indian politicians — there is a reference to "AP" against which "3 million euro" has been listed.

Another amount of 15/16 million euros was listed against "FAM" which is said to be "Family". Haschke has claimed the note was dictated to him by British consultant Michel during one of their meetings in 2008.

On Thursday, Italian prosecutor Eugenio Fusco asked Haschke during a court hearing in Busto Arsizio near Milan whether "AP" in the note was a reference to Ahmed Patel.

In his reply, the middlemen said he did not know what AP meant when he wrote it down. Haschke also denied any bribes were paid for the contract and said that the "budget sheet" was just an imaginary note drawn up and was never acted upon.

He also said the budget sheet was merely bragging by Michel about his Indian contacts and that Haschke tried to disassociate himself from the Briton.

Strongly denying any wrongdoing in the deal, Haschke also claimed to Indian interrogators in the court that no bribes were paid for the contract and that the money he received from AgustaWestland - in excess of 24 million euros - is justified as fees for engineering consultations.

Italian prosecutors also produced another note in court Thursday - a March 2008 fax by Michel to Peter Hulett, said to be the then head of region, govt sales at AgustaWestland's India office. The fax said that among the politicians who would use the choppers once acquired by India would be UPA chairperson Sonia Gandhi and her senior advisors, including Ahmed Patel.

However, Sonia is not entitled to use government helicopters. She can use VIP aircraft only when she flies with the PM, President or ministers who are officially entitled to the aircraft. This fax by the British middleman has also been shared by the Italian side with the CBI team that is in Busto Arsizio for the hearing.

Michel has been elusive and no investigative agency has been able to reach him.

Haschke, who is facing a case in Italy for being part of a conspiracy to bribe Indian officials to ensure the AW 101 chopper was picked by the IAF, faced several questions from the Indian side and denied any irregularity.

But the Indian side did not ask Haschke to explain what AP, FAM or any of the other acronyms in the note - "DS", "JS AIR", "AFA", "DG Acquisition", CVC" etc - referred to, source said.

The middleman, who was quizzed about his association with former Air Chief S P Tyagi - named as an accused in the CBI case in the deal - denied that any money had been paid to the retired Indian officer. Haschke, sources said, admitted that he was in regular touch with three cousins of Tyagi who have also been named in the case.

In response to a question from the Indian side, Haschke said he was not aware if any money was paid to S P Tyagi.

The UPA government had come under pressure in connection with the alleged kickbacks last month after The Indian Express report on the budget sheet of the middlemen. The opposition BJP had demanded the government reveal what or who "AP" and "FAM" stand for. The party also said that it wants a detailed discussion in Parliament on "alleged payments to persons close to the ruling establishment" in connection with the controversial chopper deal and has accused the government of "running away from discussions".

The discussion did not take place as the Parliament session was abruptly called off midway.

Heading: UP govt gives nod to all-woman police station for Ghaziabad - Indian Express
Content:
Restraining a woman from living in her husband's house and restricting her access to her personal belongings is a form of 'economic abuse' under the Domestic Violence Act 2005, a city court observed in its recent order.

Turning the spotlight on the extent of a woman's right over her matrimonial home, the order came while allowing an appeal by one Meena Bindra against an order of a magistrate that had dismissed her complaint on grounds of merit.

"A grave error has been committed in ignoring the relevant material on record. The complaint reveals sufficient acts of domestic violence and the act of verbal and emotional abuse have not been discussed by the trial court," Additional Sessions Judge (ASJ) Narottam Kaushal said in his order. "All the acts indicated in the complaint fall in the definition of 'domestic violence' as defined in Section 3 of the Act. Restraining her continuous access to the flat which was the shared house hold and thus prohibiting her the use of her personal effects is an economic abuse," the ASJ added.

In her complaint, Meena had alleged that she had been tricked by her husband and his mother into leaving her matrimonial home. She had gone to visit her mother and on her return, she was not allowed to enter her husband's flat in Rohini, she said. She added that her clothes, jewellery and other valuables were still lying in the flat, but her husband was restricting her from accessing those. Even her car was given to her after she got the police to intervene, Meena told the court in her complaint.

The court has now directed the trial court to "re-hear both the parties" and to proceed in accordance with the law. "The order passed by the Ld. Metropolitan Magistrate cannot be sustained. The order is absolutely merit-less and is thus set-aside. It is further directed the trial court shall immediately decide interim relief sought by the appellant," the ASJ added.

Heading: Khan Market raises own defence - Indian Express
Content:
The UP government has sanctioned the first all-woman police station for Ghaziabad. Gautam Budh Nagar already has one.

The Ghaziabad police had sent a proposal for such a police station a few months back. The UP government approved the proposal last week.

The all-woman police station is being seen as a welcome change in the district police.

"We welcome the police station in the district as there are several complex issues that the police have to deal with while handling complaints related to women or made by them. Most of the times, women constables who are not sufficient in number had to stay night long with women criminals," said a senior police official.

SSP, Ghaziabad, L Ravi Kumar said an all-women police station was long-awaited in the district.

Talking about the land allotment to the police station, he said, "Ghaziabad police have enough land and we will construct the all-woman police station in the police lines. The total land area of the police station is yet to be decided," said Kumar.

The proposed police station will have one woman inspector, two sub-inspectors, six women sub-inspectors, and 14 women constables including a driver.

"Women who have been illtreated or victimised will be able to talk about their problems freely with the women constables. There are many issues related to domestic problems. Only woman constables would be able to handle those issues effectively," added SSP.

The all-women police station was part of chief minister Mayawati's plan to open all-woman police stations in all districts of Uttar Pradesh. "We do not need land from the Ghaziabad Development Authority as we have enough land with the department," added the SSP.

Projecting its women-friendly face, the police department will also offer counselling to women who approach women police officers with their complaints.

Heading: Driving Mr Nihon - Indian Express
Content:
Shopkeepers form civil defence unit, with a little help from police

The recent blasts having re-emphasised the susceptibility of markets in the face of such attacks, South Delhi's Khan Market has decided to up its antennae. Shopkeepers have now pooled resources with the police to deal with any contingency by forming a civil defence unit among themselves.

As of now, 18 shop owners from the market have volunteered for the task and each has been assigned specific roles in the case of an emergency. These include:

* Closing shops at the earliest to ensure people are evacuated without panic

* Cordoning off the affected site from crowds

* Blocking or diverting traffic at the market's entry point to avoid bottlenecks and confusion

* Ensuring smooth vehicular movement in the area, and

* Taking measures to meet medical emergencies and rushing injured to hospitals.

The volunteers have also undergone training in fist-aid under supervision of the police.

Sanjiv Mehra, president of Khan Market Traders' Association, said shop owners decided to take these steps after being told by the police that the market is among high-risk target areas of the Capital. "These are precautionary measures to ensure we are prepared to meet any eventuality," he said.

A siren has also been put up and provisions made for a member of the civil defence force to make announcement to alert shoppers from the market's public address system. Parking attendants have also undergone special training to be on the alert, and to control traffic movements in the event of an emergency.

Last week, the police held a mock drill to rehearse the possible course of action. "The drill was organised to ensure least casualties in the event of an emergency. The market was successfully evacuated within 10 to 15 minutes," Harish Malik of the traders' association said.

Tughlaq Road SHO Anil Kumar Yadav said, "The security angle here becomes additionally important since the market is surrounded by VIP localities, and many diplomats and VIPs come here to shop."

The market association has also put up notices alerting shoppers and shopkeepers across Khan Market.

Heading: Easel by your Side - Indian Express
Content:
Auto rickshaw driver Rakesh Malhotra has picked up enough Japanese to make him popular with Japanese tourists

Many years ago, Rakesh Malhotra would drop off a student of Japanese to her institute every day in his auto rickshaw. The girl, of course, learnt the language and in the process so did Malhotra.

"For six months I ferried her to Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan from her home in Safdarjung Enclave. This was in 2004. I told her I was eager to learn Japanese and she taught me the basics. Every day, she would give me a list of 10 words to learn. She was my first guru," says Malhotra. After that initial help, Malhotra tried to learn the language himself, through books picked up from Nai Sarak.

The acquired skill is coming in handy now. Malhotra drives around Japanese tourists in the city; it fetches him handsome tips that range from Rs 100 to Rs 500.

One hand on the wheel, Malhotra gives a jaunty greeting in Japanese over the phone. His son is dropping a group of Japanese tourists to the domestic airport. "My son is also learning Japanese from Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan and he required some help with directions. So, I spoke to the tourists in Japanese and decided the fare as well," says Malhotra, pulling out a sheet of paper that has the Japanese words for airport, evening, address, entry, exit and map.

The 52-year-old's Japanese vocabulary is 300-word strong and growing. "I started learning Japanese when I found that I couldn't handle Japanese tourists, who didn't like speaking in English. With the upcoming Commonwealth Games, knowing the language will be a big asset," says Malhotra, who ran a lottery shop outside Tis Hazari before he began driving an auto rickshaw 20 years ago.

Malhotra, who says he has ferried about 3,000 Japanese tourists, usually hangs around New Delhi railway station, Connaught Place, international airport and five-star hotels, looking out for Japanese tourists. Once he spots them, he turns on the charm.

"Usually an effusive 'Mr Nihon' (Mr Japan) does the trick. Later, I crank out a string of phrases such as doko e ikkismas ka (where do you have to go?) and koni kiwa (how are you?) to break the ice," smiles Malhotra, who known how to win over Japanese tourists.

Knowing a smattering of Japanese is also helping Malhotra expand his operations from auto driver to tourist guide. He often accompanies tourists to Jaipur, Agra and Ajmer.

"I even suggest the itinerary to Japnese tourists sometimes," says Malhotra.

His association with Japanese tourists has given him some insights into their likes and dislikes. "They are different from Americans, Koreans and other nationals. No Japanese passenger has ever enquired about drug dealers. The Japanese love to talk about technology."

Not content with driving the Japanese around in India, Malhotra now wants to ferry them through Japan. "I've heard the salary there is Rs 90,000 per month. Who will let a chance like that pass?" he asks. "In the next five years, I would like to tour around Japan, China and Paris," he adds.

Heading: Gypsy Kings - Indian Express
Content:
The mall is no longer just about branded items. It's the new, popular venue for art galleries and exhibitions

The trendy FCUK designer store and Hidesign leather accessories hardly seem like the perfect backdrop for Amritsar-based artist Atul Mehra's acrylic on canvas depicting the different moods of Lord Krishna, but Adishwar Puri is convinced that when shoppers at Select Citywalk view them together during the second All India Art Trade Fair, the contrast will not seem particularly odd. "Artwork in the mall will only make the shopping experience more holistic. Besides, it will create more art enthusiasts," says Puri as he gears up to erect 45 stalls near Barista in the swish mall on October 24.

This isn't the first time when the mall, so far bereft of an art gallery, will host an exhibition, or when connoisseurs in the capital plan a trip to a mall to view artworks. As innumerable galleries mushroom across the city it isn't unfamiliar anymore to discuss brushstrokes over a glass of wine in a fine dining restaurant or to stumble upon a canvas during a shopping expedition in the neighbourhood mall. While SH Raza's bindu and John Tun Sein's abstract greeted guests who trooped in for the opening show of Passage Art Gallery located above the restaurant Crepes and More in Khan market on Friday evening, Sharon Apparao is looking forward to dressing the walls at DLF Emporio with artwork by Farhan Mujib in an exhibition starting October 17. This comes within a month of her previous exhibition at the same venue that had artworks by N Ramachandran, Atul Dodiya and Alexis Kersey in a curated group show titled 'The Demonic and the Divine'. "We have always been open to experimenting with unconventional spaces," says Apparao. "Not every mall makes an appropriate venue but people frequenting Emporio are the kinds who appreciate and understand art."

While Apparao is targeting the high-end circuit at the glitzy new mall at TDI in Rajouri Gardens, Sonia Kathuria, assistant vice president, marketing, is hoping to provide a platform for local craftsmen to display their work. "This is an added service and monetary benefit is not the motive. The regular rental rates are exorbitant, but we only charge craftsmen for basic infrastructure," says Kathuria. Rajiv Duggal, CEO of Select Citywalk adds, "One need not always exhibit artwork by renowned artists. The aim is to give a flavour of art to the shoppers. We intend to showcase work that is affordable."

However, unlike a gallery where spectators expect artwork, malls do have to put in extra effort to make certain that frames suspended in the passages attract attention. "We choose work that is visually stimulating, but people need to take a moment out to reflect on them," says Shah. Clearly, casaul shoppers have a dormant interest in art. Dr Akhter Husain recently displayed his canvases at the Select Citywalk atrium in an exhibition titled 'Pigments and Pictures'. "The sales are encouraging and there were several queries," he says. Brigadier (retd) Deepak Kapur, general manager of mall operations at Ambience mall, Gurgaon says he prefers to keep art separate from the luxury stores. So at his mall, a 30,000 sq ft hall has been constructed specifically for art exhibitions. "We are still finalising details but there will be shows in this space soon," says Kapur. Mall rats turn art connoisseurs? That may not be so odd anymore.

Heading: Tandoor Tidings - Indian Express
Content:
The musicians from Hungary who made gypsy rhythms popular worldwide, are in India to trace their roots

Eight years ago Europe discovered a new kind of music — gypsy rhythms from a remote corner of Hungary. Fresh and folksy, catchy and danceable, listeners couldn't stop moving to the beats. Critics found to their amusement, much of the sound came from instruments like spoons and milk cans. The tracks climbed up the charts and the group, Parno Graszt (meaning White Horse in native Romani), became the first Hungarian band ever to feature in the European top ten countdown. Ever since, Parno Graszt has been an essential part of almost all major musical festivals in Europe, from the Netherlands and France, to Russia and Belgium. For the next few weeks, however, the world's favourite gypsies are on a new trip— to discover their roots in India.

"Our forefathers left India more than 2,000 years ago and some Rajasthan dialects have similar sounding words to ours. We're travelling back on the path our people came from," says band member Jozsef Olah, during a brief stopover in Delhi on route to Jaipur. While in Jaipur, they will perform with an indigenous group from Rajasthan at a music function. Accompanying them is a film crew from BBC which is making its second documentary on the group.

At the Old Delhi railway station, the band's luggage has all the expected musical accompaniments— guitar, accordion, more guitars as well as some peculiarly shaped instruments like kitchen pincers. "Anything that can be used to create sound is an instrument for us. We've even rubbed our fingers on door surfaces to create melody," says Olah, who plays the tambourine and guitar. The songs deal with love and loss and pleasant pastimes like fishing and usually, the beats are infused with joy.

Parno Graszt was formed in 1987 in Szabolcs-Szatmar-Bereg, one of the most underdeveloped counties of Hungary. The lack of modernity, however, had one positive result; the ethnic culture of the gypsy Roma community remained intact.

In a typical gathering, everybody in the community grabs an instrument and plays along. "Nobody in our group has ever trained in music. My mother Erzsebet Nemeth envisioned a band and goaded me to form one that would sing our kind of music," says Olah. All of Parno Graszt's members are from Olah's family; his elder brother Janos is on double bass and vocals, his son Krisztian on the accordion and his nephew Viktor on the guitar. All of them remain part of the band, even though of the 24 members, only five have come to India. Olah begins to strum his guitar as band member Sandor Horvath beats a sound out of the kitchen pincers. And then, they burst into song.

Parno Graszt will perform at IIC on October 19 at 6.30 pm. Contact: 24619431

Heading: Ready for life - Indian Express
Content:
Yet another restaurant recreates popular Mughlai recipes

On a Friday afternoon we headed to the newly opened restaurant Orange Hara in west Delhi (named after the orange glow of the sun). It was packed with ladies since Friday is kitty party day, however, the relentless chatter gave the place some buzz and ambience. The menu is a mix of typical North Indian curries and interesting kebab recipes. Chef Ghanim Bin Hairat, after spending several years at The Great Kebab Factory has carefully drafted the menu at Orange Haara keeping in mind the favourites of Delhiites and he's added a little extra something for the adventurous foodie.

Must try
The liquor license is yet to come but the mocktail bar seems well stocked. Right now you can choose between cranberry apple virgin mojito or a spicy tamarind cooler. We tried virgin dark grape capriosska (Rs 125). The grape juice, soda and lemon mix gelled perfectly with our platter of kebabs. The Neza kebab (Rs 450), is the restaurant speciality. A platter of tandoori prawns (Rs 595) is another delicious starter with bright yellow portions of the fish brushed with a creamy yoghurt based marinade. Mattarwali tikki (Rs 225) is exceptionally well done with pan-grilled portions of patties stuffed with green peas, mint and cheese. Among entrées, Nalli Gosht (Rs 425) and Khada palak paneer (Rs 225) stand out among the options. A robust and traditional curry, Orange Hara offers nalli gosht with a Punjabi twang.

Give a miss
Tandoori Salad (Rs 225) with grilled chunks of cottage cheese, bell peppers and fresh pineapple was disappointing. Vegetarians, it seems, are not high on the priority list.

Meal for two: Rs 1,800

Contact: 25161647

Location: Ground Floor, Paragon Mall, Rajouri Garden

Heading: An eventful journey - Indian Express
Content:
A special school prepares learning-disabled children to face the world through vocational training

With its spacious playground and its classrooms full of drawings by children, it looks like any other school. But instead of learning to solve mathematical problems or reading literature, students of the Aanchal School at Chanakyapuri are learning paper craft, tailoring and carpentry. The aim is to make these special children with learning disabilities self-sufficient. Downstairs, a music teacher plays the piano while a few students sing and play the dholak and students over 18 attend vocational training classes. Colourful envelopes, paper bags and candles made by them will be sold in Dilli Haat.

At the end of their stay in school, students know how to present themselves and give their address and phone number if the need arises. "Once they leave the school, most of them are self-sufficient," says special educator B. Uma.

But even after the children have been trained, many of them would still have trouble speaking, handling money or travelling alone. Only a few of them have managed to get jobs.

The school's special educators also counsel parents on how to deal with the problems of their children. "Some parents are not able to figure out that their child has a disability," explains occupational therapist Poonam Vig. Even those who are aware of their children's disability don't know to deal with it. "They tend to be either too protective or to neglect the children," says Vig.

The role of the family is something the special educators never tire of emphasising.

Heading: Cooking up an idea - Indian Express
Content:
Running a website that is the ultimate guide to the cultural activities in Delhi is Rohit Malik's way of promoting art

Rohit Malik has never spent a lonely evening. And he doesn't quite understand why anybody else should. For the 30-year-old owner of www.delhievents.com, the city is a colourful collage of constant activity.

For the past two years, his website has been listing all the happening activities in the Capital—from street plays to food festivals, from salsa to soirees, from workshops to trade fairs. "Whatever your interest, there's always a show that you won't want to miss," says Malik.

That explains why Delhievents gets thousands of hits, from expats who want an instant flavour of the city, to students who want to know what's new and Mandi House regulars planning the week ahead.

"The site is updated the moment fresh information of an event comes in, sometimes very late at night," says Malik, who is often the first to get such news, even before the newspapers and magazines. Meetu Kapur, gallery coordinator of The Stainless, calls the site "a big help, especially since the information is up five minutes after I send out the mailers."

Several listings, especially of theatre, have not only detailed descriptions but also audio interviews with the director. Malik tracks events with the kind of zeal with which his friends from his IT diploma days track the stock market.

"Unfortunately, the website is no cash cow," he says. Delhievents, with just one sponsor, earns him practically nothing. Yet, Malik has turned down job offers, lobbed taunts from his relatives and broken every expectation of his parents to focus on his website. What others would describe as a labour of love, he calls an obsession. His school friends are running small businesses but Malik potters away in his small room, on his assembled desktop computer.

He points to a picture of Osho on the wall in front of his computer. "He said that we should promote good things like art and culture without worrying about results. That gives me hope and keeps me going when I get frustrated," says Malik, who has spent several months at the Osho commune in Pune.

His day starts early, with calls to event managers, theatre directors and cultural honchos. "Initially, I would run around venues to meet people who do important and interesting things. Most people appreciated my interest though few understood what it was that I was trying to do," Malik says. "These days, most of the information comes to me." But he still frequents rehearsals to get a better idea and "decide if it's worth the audience's time and money."

A recent addition to his site is a section highlighting important art events through thumbnail pictures. "One of the main purposes of the site is to give the arts a push. Classical dancers, musicians and stage artistes put in their whole lives to perfect themselves," he says.

Recently, however, one artist found his exhibition yanked off the thumbnails "because he had succumbed to the morality police and removed some pictures. I would have expected artists to be more brave." Perhaps like himself.

Heading: NDMC to pay compensation 13 yrs after boy drowned in lake - Indian Express
Content:
A lunch delivery service launched by management graduates has roped in housewives to serve up nutritional dishes right out of mom's kitchen

Mumbai's dabbawallas are counted among the smartest management gurus in India. Now meet Samarth Gupta, 25, and Pawan Verma, 30, management graduates from Indian Management Institute, Delhi, who have come up with 'Poshan', an initiative that has at its core a network of housewives—chosen through a cookery competition—who provide healthy vegetarian food to those who don't have access to ghar ka khana.

The idea was conceived in their college days, during lessons in strategy formulation, when the duo realised that the "food industry is never really going to face any sort of recession". This confidence is what made Gupta and Verma give the campus placement interviews a miss. "We wanted to make housewives with good cookery skills financially independent," says Verma. Says Yuvika Chejera, who is part of Poshan's team of 12 housewives, "I did not want my culinary skills to go waste. This is a good way to make use of my free time." The women take turns, with two of them cooking in a day.

Gupta says the service, which hopes to help those who are away from their families feel at home, is "a passion with a purpose". Poshan has a big menu and serves up dishes that are right out of mom's kitchen. There is an assortment of everyday delicacies like rajma chawal, aloo matar, tinde, torai, aloo-gobhi and simple dals. The paneer preparations are not made with heavy gravies and spices, which is how restaurants serve them. "The idea is to provide food that tastes exactly like one's mother would make it, taking care not to make it too oily or spicy," says Verma.

In the age of grab-and-go eateries, these hygienic and nutritional dabbas, priced reasonably at Rs 55, are an ideal alternative to fast food. "Convenience foods don't come cheap and many are bad for health. We have proper quality check systems at the base kitchen and the distribution centres," says Gupta. The base kitchen is in Patpargarj, but the distribution centre is located near Barakhamba Road, Connaught Place, for effective delivery.

The service, which primarily caters to office-goers in and around Connaught Place, delivers more than 200 well-packed boxes of food every day. Expansion plans are in the pipeline. "We are going to cater to other areas in the city soon, and also introduce a dinner facility by November," say Gupta and Verma.

Management gurus with a difference, they are only too happy to share the secret of their success. "Do your work with dedication. We provide food and we take pride in that."

Heading: Former BJP councillor shot dead - Indian Express
Content:
Keeping the hopes of a tie-up with the Congress in Uttar Pradesh alive, Samajwadi Party (SP) president Mulayam Singh Yadav on Saturday said his party will soon sort out seat-sharing issues to defeat the "nefarious designs" of communal forces.

Addressing a rally in Mainpuri, the former chief minister alleged that wrong economic policies of the Mayawati Government, leading to spiraling prices of essential commodities, had made lives of the people "miserable."

Speaking at Bhongaon Nation Degree College ground, he said, "The (state) government is doing nothing for the welfare of the people. It is busy erecting statues of Kanshiram and Mayawati."

Alleging that there was blatant misuse of the Harijan Act, he said atrocities against Dalits had soared. The law and order situation in the state has deteriorated, resulting in growing incidents of rape, murder and kidnapping, he charged. Condemning atrocities against minorities in Maharashtra, Karnataka and Orissa, he said the BJP and its off-shoot Bajrang Dal were trying to gain political mileage by fomenting communal flare-up.

Heading: Blueline mows down 25-yr-old - Indian Express
Content:
Former BJP councillor Raghubir Kuchhal was shot dead late on Saturday evening. According to sources, Kucchal was near his medical store in Vijaynagar Ghaziabad when the two motorcyclists shot at him and fled.

As news spread, BJP party workers and leaders flooded Yashoda Hospital in Kaushambi. The wife of the murdered ex-councillor, Bimla Kucchal, is the sitting BJP councillor from Vijaynagar. "Kuchhal was dead by the time he was brought to the hospital. He was shot in the stomach and excessive bleeding could be the reason for his death," said doctors at the hospital.

Party workers said the incident took place around 8 pm when Kucchal was about to close his shop. "He was outside his shop when he was shot by unknown assailants. He had no enemies and was a popular BJP member. He became BJP councillor from Vijaynagar in 1995. He was state minister of the local cell of BJP looking after all major developments in the region," said S P Singh, media co-ordinator, BJP, western UP.

SSP, L Ravi Kumar said, "We hope to make arrests soon." A senior police official said some people had a property dispute with Kucchal and the assailants have been identified.

Heading: Sushma to Sheila: What time, place is safe for women to drive alone? - Indian Express
Content:
A 25-year-old youth was crushed to death by a Blueline bus in Noida's Sector 11 on Saturday. The police said the incident occurred when the Blueline tried to overtake another Blueline bus on the same route and hit a motorcyclist, a resident of Bihar, leaving him dead on the spot.

The incident occurred around 8 pm. "The motorcyclist was standing just next to a Blueline bus. The bus driver that crushed the motorcyclist could not see him and dragged him along as he was driving at a high speed," Devendra Kumar, Sector 24 station house officer, said.

The victim, Ompal singh, was resident of Mamura village in Noida. He was rushed to the Metro Hospital. "He was declared dead on arrival. A case of rash driving causing death has been registered against the absconding driver," Kumar said.

Heading: Child labour banned? Ask Karan - Indian Express
Content:
After price rise and lack of security in the Capital, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), it seems, has struck upon another issue ahead of the Assembly elections later this year: Chief Minister Sheila Dikshit's comments on the mystery death of Headlines Today journalist Soumya Vishwanathan.

Widely seen as insensitive, and that too coming from a woman, party leader Sush Swaraj took on Dikshit on her statement at a symposium on women's security held on Saturday. "If Sheila-ji feels Soumya was being adventurous returning home at 3 am, then we should ask her what time and which part of the city she thinks is safe for women," Swaraj said

BJP's chief ministerial candidate V K Malhotra and state unit chief Dr Harsh Vardhan were among other leaders present at the event.

After Vishwanathan, 26, was found shot dead in her car in the early hours of September 30, Dikshit had said, "All by herself till 3 am at night in a city where people believe — you know — you should not be so adventurous."

Malhotra said, "We have repeatedly said that full statehood is absolutely necessary for progress of Delhi."

Swaraj suggested the police post women constables as decoy during night to curb teasing and molestation.

Heading: Tech institute holds robotics workshop - Indian Express
Content:
Twelve-year-old Karan has been making Ravana effigies for the past three years. He gets Rs 100 for working all day, which includes getting provisions, painting and cleaning up afterwards. While he has been working since the age of nine, he does manage to go to a nearby government school, and makes the effigies after school. He has three younger siblings and his father works as a sweeper in the same locality.

"I give Rs 80 to my mother and put Rs 20 in my piggy bank. I will buy new clothes for Diwali," Karan says, not quite aware he is a child labourer, termed "unlawful" by the 2006 Amendment of the Child Labour Protection Act.

The Amendment led to the inclusion of child domestic labour as a hazardous form of child labour.

But millions of children still work under hazardous conditions, are missing from home and remain untraceable.

Since the Amendment, the total number of prosecutions till date, according to the Union Ministry of Labour, stands at 1,680, with a total of 6,782 children being rescued. The child labour force in India is bigger than anywhere else in the world. Official statistics put the total number of children working at 1.3 crore. Unofficial figures vary between 6 and 10 crore.

Thomas Chandy, CEO, Save the Children - Bal Raksha Bharat, says: "With the Amendment banning the employment of children under 14 as domestic workers, we have seen an increase in inspections and rescue efforts. But with nearly 1 million children working in Delhi alone as domestic workers, clearly much still needs to be done to ensure that the law is implemented and acts as a deterrent to employers."

Heading: 25-year-old woman found dead, husband absconding - Indian Express
Content:
The Netaji Subhash Institute of Technology (NSIT) in Dwarka organised Robokriti, a series of robotics workshops in collaboration with Technophilia Solutions, in Delhi on October 4 and 5.

Similar workshops were organised in Gwalior, Indore, PEC Chandigarh, Dehradun, and ITM (Gurgaon) between September and October.

Innovision 2008, an annual technical and Business fest, will be held between October 16 and 18. The fest will see a number of events that will test the capability of the participants to create powerful robots and machines.

The workshop focussed on four kinds of robotic technologies: wired robotics, i.e. robots controlled through switches; wireless robotics, where robots are remote controlled; computer controlled robotics and speech-controlled robotics. "Speech Control" was an important aspect of the workshop, where technology that allows for controlling robots via spoken commands was showcased. It is a new addition to school-level robotics events.

Robokriti was designed to enable students to learn the basic concepts of robotics and gain practical experience by working with robotics kit designed by Technophilia. The workshop also helped the students understand basic electronics, mechanics and computer programming required for robot motion control.

Robots built by participants competed in preliminary and zonal level competitions, and winners will now take part in the final event during the NSIT fest. The winner at Innovision will also get a direct entry into IIT-Bombay's Techfest.

Heading: City changes signal - Indian Express
Content:
A 25-year-old woman's highly decomposed body was found on her bed in her house in Trilokpuri on Friday night. Police said Sangeeta Devi, seems to have been murdered and her husband, Sanjay Pawar, is on the run. The victim's family alleged her husband used to harass her for dowry. Police said on Friday, Sangeeta's neighbour, Ramesh Kumar went to check as a foul smell was coming out of the house. He then called the PCR.

"Sangeeta's body was found in her bedroom," said a senior police official. Her father, Suresh Kumar said, "She used to come home saying he had beaten her up and was demanding dowry." Sanjay is an executive with ICICI Bank in Badarpur.

Heading: Armed robbers hit trader family in Hauz Khas - Indian Express
Content:
GSM technology to send instant alert for repair, timers to blink as per red/green light

One of the busiest traffic intersections in the area, Ashirwad Chowk in Dwarka is looking spanking new since October 1. And with good reason: the junction has got rid of the boring yellow-painted traffic signals and replaced them with hi-tech ones hanging from a cantilever, an overhead pole running parallel to the road.

The new traffic signs, motorists crossing the intersection say, is visible from a fairly long distance.

This, then, is the Capital's first tryst with GSM-based automatic fault monitoring system, which ensures the maintaining authority gets the reason for a fault within minutes of the signal going kaput. Another big advantage is power backup for the signals; this means powercuts would not leave traffic at the intersection blind.

This, incidentally, is also the first time that a traffic signal has been installed in the city by a firm other than CMS and Keltron, which, between themselves, manage all of Delhi's 710 traffic signals and 435 blinkers. Installed by Onnyx Electronics, which maintains traffic signals in Kolkata too, the system would be replicated across Delhi after a review of the "sample", Joint Commissioner (Traffic) S N Shrivastava said.

"We have installed the traffic signal as a sample and will maintain it for next three years for free," Onnyx Electronics' CEO Jitendra Kaushik said.

Besides the fault monitoring system, the new signal has, for the first time, dual coloured timers. This means when the light is green the timer at the intersection will also be green, and the same in case of red light. It also has different signals for each lane to promote lane-wise signalling.

"We have noticed that drivers tend to automatically stick to a lane for either right or left turn when they see the arrow twinkling from a distance," Kaushik said. "This reduces conflict."

To save the traffic intersection from usual cable fault due to moisture, which hits nearly 80 per cent of traffic intersections during rains, the controller has been set up in separate manholes, constructed at a significant height. The poles are thicker to ensure that the signal does not fall during heavy showers or a squal.

The poles have not been put in by digging up earth, Kaushik said, instead it is fixed with nuts and bolts. "This is to ensure that it takes less time to replace the poles in case of an accident," he said. "They can also easily be shifted."

Heading: In Ghaziabad, 14-year-old ‘raped’ by head constable - Indian Express
Content:
House opposite DCP office; Rs 3 lakh cash, jewellery worth Rs 30 lakh gone

Armed robbers barged into the house of a chartered accountant on Friday in Hauz Khas in South Delhi and robbed Rs 3 lakh and jewellery worth Rs 30 lakh. They were reportedly armed with screwdrivers and knives.

A case of robbery has been registered with Hauz Khas police station. Several teams are working in the case but no arrests have been made even 24 hours after the incident.

The robbery took place around 2 pm yesterday at the G-25 Hauz Khas, opposite the district DCP office. The house belongs to Sanjay Mitra, a chartered accountant. Mitra was not home as he had gone out for work. His wife Bindu, his son and a servant were at home when the robbers broke in. They were attacked for resisting.

The robbers, all aged between 25 and 30, entered the house and allegedly locked it from inside. They then asked Bindu to give them keys of the almirah's locker and when she refused, they attacked her and her son. Bindu received minor injury in her head. The domestic help who tried to save them but was also beaten up.

The robbers then stripped the safe of all cash and jewellery and fled threatening the family with dire consequences.

Bindu informed her husband who called the police. The family is making estimates of their loss. Mitra told the police it was around Rs 40 lakh.

Bindu is helping the police make sketches of suspects. Photographs of some local criminals are being shown to her.

A senior South district official said they have identified a few suspects but their names could not be disclosed without verification. "We have clues. The accused were either informed by somebody very close to the family about the cash and jewellery are kept in the house or they had been following Mitra," said a police official.

Mitra's wife Bindu is a trading agent. District DCP HGS Dhaliwal was not available for comment.

Heading: Another alert at IGI: A-I flight lands with smoke in cockpit - Indian Express
Content:
A 14-year-old girl was allegedly raped by a head constable of Uttar Pradesh Police on Friday evening at the Sahibabad Police quarters. A case of kidnapping and rape has been registered against the accused who is on the run. Ghaziabad Police said the services of the accused, Shyam Lal, have been terminated and a case has been registered with the Bhajanpura (Delhi) police station.

Delhi Police officials said Lal first met the girl and her family around nine months back in a criminal breach of trust case that the family had filed in Sahibabad. After that they became family friends.
